    • Check the planned movement of the tool and carriage against the chuck, workpiece and supports.
    • Locate the emergency stop and foot brake, and confirm how to operate them before starting.

    A long unsupported bar can whip as it rotates. Support at the cutting end does not establish that the part behind the spindle is safe.

    The whole workpiece rotates; chip strings can catch and cut

    The whole workpiece rotates; chip strings can catch and cut

    The chuck, workpiece and any material projecting from the spindle are rotating hazards. Apply the entanglement rules to the entire setup, including its back side.

    In our labs, stop and clear long chip strings when they become a hazard. Never pull a chip string by hand. Use Metal Chips and Swarf for removal and cleanup. If long strings keep forming, have the instructor review the cutting setup before continuing.

    If the work shifts or the setup behaves unexpectedly, stop safely

    If the work shifts or the setup behaves unexpectedly, stop safely

    Do not try to steady rotating work or catch a loose part. Use the stopping controls you were shown if you can reach them safely, keep clear, and notify the instructor. Use Lab Conduct and Emergencies for an injury or emergency.

    Finish with the shutdown procedure and chip cleanup. A stopped spindle is required before measuring or changing the setup; maintenance requires the isolation procedure in Machine Hazards and Housekeeping.

    Safety/Equipment

    Vertical Mill

    Check workholding, cutter clearance and cutting settings; recognize the different categories for manual and CNC mills.

    Manual mill: Category 3; CNC mill: Category 2 in the Metals lab

    Manual mill: Category 3; CNC mill: Category 2 in the Metals lab

    A vertical mill uses a rotating cutter to remove material held in a vise or clamps. See Vertical Mill Anatomy and Motion for the machine's parts.

    The manual mill is Category 3 in the Metals lab; the CNC mill is Category 2 there. Use Equipment Categories and Supervision for the corresponding permission and supervision requirements.

    Start with Equipment Operating Procedure, Personal Protective Equipment, Machine Hazards and Housekeeping and Metal Chips and Swarf. For the Tormach workflow, use Vertical Mill Startup, Setup and Shutdown; its controller sequence is not a startup sequence for a manual mill.

    Check clamping, cutter travel and cutting settings before the cut; Checklist

    Check clamping, cutter travel and cutting settings before the cut

    In our labs, check and recheck the workpiece clamping before beginning an operation.

    • Check the vise or clamps and the cutter's retention. Confirm the tool can follow the planned path without striking the workholding.
    • Identify the closing gaps between the moving table, workholding and machine frame. Keep the planned travel clear.
    • Check spindle speed, feed, depth of cut and width of cut for the planned operation.
    • Check coolant and slide lubrication as directed for the installed mill. Report low levels, damage or a maintenance need rather than adjusting the machine's sliding fits yourself.
    • Complete the installed mill's guard and emergency-stop checks from Equipment Operating Procedure and Machine Hazards and Housekeeping.
    A rotating cutter and a moving table create different hazards

    A rotating cutter and a moving table create different hazards

    The cutter can cut or catch what touches it; the table can close a gap against the column, vise or clamps. Keep clear of both the cutting area and the table's travel. CNC motion follows the program, so a pause in motion is not permission to reach in.

    Use Machine Hazards and Housekeeping for stopping before measurements and for isolation before adjustments or maintenance. Use Metal Chips and Swarf for chip removal, including the required controls if compressed air is used.

    If a tool breaks or the work comes loose, step away

    If a tool breaks or the work comes loose, step away

    In our labs, step away if a tool breaks or the workpiece becomes loose. Stop the mill if it is safe to do so; do not endanger yourself to reach a control. Notify the instructor in every case.

    If injured, ask for help and follow Lab Conduct and Emergencies. For normal shutdown use the installed mill's procedure and Equipment Operating Procedure; the Tormach sequence is in Vertical Mill Startup, Setup and Shutdown.

    Safety/Equipment

    OMAX Waterjet

    The lab's CAD-to-cut sequence: prepare the path, verify material settings, follow the setup prompts and dry-run before cutting.

    Waterjet: Category 2 in the Metals lab

    Waterjet: Category 2 in the Metals lab

    The waterjet cuts a programmed shape with water and abrasive. See Laser, Waterjet and Plasma Cutting for how abrasive waterjet cutting works.

    Category 2 in the Metals lab. Follow Equipment Categories and Supervision for permission and supervision, and complete Equipment Operating Procedure and Personal Protective Equipment.

    Keep hands away from the cutting nozzle and clear of its travel. The jet cuts material, and the moving head can trap a hand. See Machine Hazards and Housekeeping for movement, guards and stopping. OMAX safety information is further reading for the installed-machine training.

    Prepare the file and toolpath: lab steps 1–10

    Prepare the file and toolpath: lab steps 1–10

    This is our lab's OMAX operating sequence. Follow it with the machine-specific instruction you received at checkout.

    1. Export the CAD file to DXF or DWG, as for a laser-cut part.
    2. Turn on the OMAX machine.
    3. Turn on the water: the top water line under the sink.
    4. Open ProtoMAX Layout software.
    5. Click File → “Open file for other CAD software.”
    6. Use the move, rotate and duplicate tools to lay out the parts. One square is equal to one inch.
    7. Click Autopath to create toolpaths. Check that the path cuts on the correct side of each line and cuts inside items before outside items, so the part is not cut loose before its interior features are cut.
    8. Click Post.
    9. Select the starting position, normally the bottom left.
    10. Save the post. It saves as an .omax file.
    Verify settings, follow the prompts and dry-run: lab steps 11–15

    Verify settings, follow the prompts and dry-run: lab steps 11–15

    1. Right-click on Post and open the .omax file in ProtoMAX Make.
    2. When Make asks for cutting parameters, select the appropriate material and enter its thickness. The lab procedure says to oversize the thickness “by just a bit”; confirm that allowance with the instructor.
    3. If the machine was just turned on, Make shows a red homing button at the top of the screen. Make sure nothing obstructs the nozzle's movement before clicking it to home the machine.
    4. Follow all the on-screen steps. These include, but are not limited to:
      1. Attaching the abrasive hose.
      2. Testing the nozzle for abrasive flow.
      3. Placing and securing the material.
      4. Homing the nozzle to the starting position on the material.
      5. Adjusting the water height if necessary.
      6. Dry-running the program.
      7. Flipping down the splash guard.
    5. Run the program.

    In step 14, “homing” to the material means the job's starting position; it is distinct from the machine-homing step in step 13. Have both positions demonstrated during checkout.

    A dropped part or a fault needs a safe stop, not a reach into the tank

    A dropped part or a fault needs a safe stop, not a reach into the tank

    Do not reach into the cutting area to retrieve a part while the machine is operating. If the material moves or the cut behaves unexpectedly, keep clear and use the stopping procedure demonstrated during checkout. Notify the instructor; follow Lab Conduct and Emergencies for an emergency.

    The lab sequence above ends at running the program. Have the instructor demonstrate shutdown and safe part recovery before using the machine; a part falling into the tank is not a recovery procedure. Use Equipment Operating Procedure for the general shutdown and reporting requirements.

    Safety/Equipment

    Prusa 3D Printers

    Obtain project approval, match the sliced file to the printer and filament, and physically check the machine before setting it ready.

    3D printers: Category 1 in the Rapid Prototyping Center

    3D printers: Category 1 in the Rapid Prototyping Center

    These printers build parts from filament, layer by layer. See 3D Printing from CAD for preparing a model and FDM 3D Printing for the printing process.

    Category 1 in the Rapid Prototyping Center. Use Equipment Categories and Supervision for permission and supervision. General checks and protective equipment are in Equipment Operating Procedure and Personal Protective Equipment.

    Get the project and material approved before printing

    Get the project and material approved before printing

    In our labs, a DET faculty member must approve a 3D-printing project before it starts. A project assigned by DET faculty needs no separate project approval, but must stay within its own guidelines and all RPC rules.

    For approval, explain what the item is, where its design came from, how it will be made, the material amount and source, and its intended use; supply the digital file through the instructor's designated channel.

    • No personal material without prior approval.
    • No weapons, weapon-like items, weapon components, ammunition, dangerous materials or drug paraphernalia.
    • No commercial use. Class projects take priority over personal projects.
    Slice for the selected printer, then check it in person; Checklist

    Slice for the selected printer, then check it in person

    1. In PrusaSlicer, arrange and orient the model. Select the printer and filament, and set supports, infill and brim as needed. Slice, review the preview, material use and estimated time, then export the .gcode or .bgcode file.
    2. Use the lab's private job-identification instructions to name the file. In Prusa Connect, select a printer matching the type used when slicing.
    3. Check that printer's queue before uploading the file. In our labs, talk with the uploader before deleting a named job you think is no longer needed.
    4. Upload the file to the selected printer's dashboard, or use the guide's Send to Connect workflow from PrusaSlicer.

    Before choosing Set Ready and Print Now, go to the machine and check:

    • The build plate is clear.
    • The loaded filament type matches the sliced file.
    • There is enough filament for the job.

    If you are unsure the machine is ready, choose Add to print queue and check it before setting it ready later.

    Hot surfaces and moving parts remain hazards during remote printing

    Hot surfaces and moving parts remain hazards during remote printing

    The nozzle and heated bed can burn, including after motion stops. Let them cool before handling the finished print or build plate. Keep hands and tools out of the printer's moving area; use Machine Hazards and Housekeeping for the general movement and isolation rules. See Prusa's hot-part precautions for further reading, not permission to service lab equipment.

    The lab guide uses Prusa Connect or its app to monitor progress. A remote status display does not replace the physical readiness check. Set Ready can release the next queued job, so use it only after checking the machine and clearing the work area.

    When your print is finished and safe to handle, remove it, check the plate and material again, and set the printer ready for the next job. Remove scrap and purged filament, return tools and leave the work area tidy.

    Report jams and faults; do not repair the printer yourself

    Report jams and faults; do not repair the printer yourself

    In our labs, report jams, malfunctions and other technical problems to DET faculty. Do not try to fix equipment yourself. Stop a failing print using the controls covered in your training, and do not set a faulty printer ready for another job.

    The student guide permits resetting an offline printer only when it is not currently in use. If you cannot establish that, or if a fault remains, report it rather than repeatedly resetting. Use Lab Conduct and Emergencies for an injury or emergency.

    Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations

    What Is Manufacturing?

    Turn materials into useful products by choosing processes that fit the material, quantity, cost and required quality.

    Manufacturing turns materials into useful products

    Manufacturing turns materials into useful products

    Manufacturing changes materials into parts and products people can use. A board becomes a shelf, plastic pellets become a bottle, and metal sheet becomes a bracket. Shape, properties, joints and surfaces all contribute to the result.

    A process is an operation that makes one of those changes. Most products need several processes. A useful plan states what each operation must achieve and how the result will be checked.

    Two organizing questions keep the subject manageable: What is the material? Use the four material families. What change are we making? Use the five process categories.

    Primary processing makes usable material; secondary processing makes parts

    Primary processing makes usable material; secondary processing makes parts

    Primary processing converts raw resources into usable materials and common supply forms. Secondary processing turns those materials into parts or products. Stock means material supplied for further work, such as sheet, rod, boards or pellets.

    Metal
    Ore is refined into metal and made into stock such as sheet; sheet is then cut and bent into a bracket.
    Plastic
    Chemical feedstocks are made into polymer resin, often supplied as pellets; pellets are then molded into a bottle cap.
    Wood
    Logs are sawn into lumber; boards are then cut, joined and finished as furniture.
    Glass
    Mineral ingredients are melted and made into sheet glass; sheets are then cut and edge-finished for a window.

    These terms describe a material's place in the supply chain. They do not replace the five process categories: sawing a log and sawing a furniture part are both separating.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 17 — Why the boundary needs context.

    Choose a process that fits material, quantity, cost and quality

    Choose a process that fits material, quantity, cost and quality

    Material
    Can it tolerate the heat, force or chemical exposure? A process that bends metal sheet may crack a ceramic plate.
    Quantity
    A few parts favor flexible methods with little dedicated tooling. Repeated production can justify a mold or other tool made specifically for that part.
    Cost
    Count material, setup, tooling, labor, processing time, scrap and inspection. Cheap starting material can be expensive to turn into an acceptable part.
    Required quality
    Specify dimensions, allowable variation, strength and surface condition. Choose a route that can meet them consistently, then verify it.

    For a small plastic cover, 3D printing may be useful for a few trial pieces; molding may suit repeated production after the design settles. Neither route wins from quantity alone: material behavior, geometry and acceptance requirements still matter.

    Prototype, batch and mass production describe production situations, not universal numerical cutoffs. Manufacturing economics and design for manufacturing develop this comparison further.

    Use Measurement Language to state dimensions clearly. 5S Workplace Organization explains how organized tools and materials support repeatable work.

    Read every material unit through the same six-stage map

    Read every material unit through the same six-stage map

    Characteristics → Forming → Separating → Fabricating → Conditioning → Finishing

    1. Characteristics: What is the material like? Compare properties, useful forms and limitations.
    2. Forming: How can it take a shape?
    3. Separating: How can material be removed or cut apart?
    4. Fabricating: How can parts be joined?
    5. Conditioning: How can its internal properties be changed?
    6. Finishing: How can its surface be protected or improved?

    This is the collection's learning map for the later plastics, wood and metals topics. Characteristics is the starting description, not a sixth process category.

    The map is not a mandatory factory sequence. Wood may be dried before cutting; a metal part may be annealed between forming steps; some surfaces are finished before assembly. A product may repeat a category or omit one.

    Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations

    Manufacturing Process Categories

    Classify an operation by its main purpose: separating, forming, fabricating, conditioning or finishing.

    Five categories describe the change an operation makes

    Five categories describe the change an operation makes

    Name the operation's intended result. Are we removing material, creating shape, joining parts, changing internal properties or treating a surface?

    This collection uses the course's five-category model. In this model, forming includes casting, molding and additive manufacturing such as 3D printing. Other technical references may separate those into their own process groups.

    Separating removes material to make a size, shape or opening

    Separating removes material to make a size, shape or opening

    Separating cuts material apart or removes it from a workpiece, the piece being worked on. Look for a cut edge, hole, slot or reduced dimension as the intended result.

    • Sawing: cut a wooden board or plastic rod to length.
    • Drilling: remove material to make a hole in a metal bracket or wooden panel.
    • Milling: a rotating cutter removes material to make a flat face, pocket or slot.
    • Laser cutting: remove material along a narrow path to cut a suitable sheet material.

    For metal-cutting examples, continue to Milling Operations and Lathe Operations. The tool motions differ, but both remove material.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 18 — A laser cut does not have to vaporize all the removed material.

    Forming creates shape without using material removal as the shaping method

    Forming creates shape without using material removal as the shaping method

    Forming gives material a shape by filling a mold, deforming it or building it up. The central action creates the shape rather than cutting unwanted material away.

    • Casting and molding: pour metal into a mold, mold a plastic cap, or cast a concrete planter.
    • Bending: bend sheet metal into a bracket or bend prepared wood around a form.
    • Forging: press or hammer metal into a new shape.
    • 3D printing: build a plastic part in layers.

    Forming can still produce excess material. Trimming a molded edge or cutting away printed supports is a separate separating operation. “Forming” does not promise zero waste.

    Fabricating joins parts into an assembly

    Fabricating joins parts into an assembly

    Fabricating brings separate parts together so they work as one assembly. Ask whether the intended result is a joint.

    • Welding: join metal frame members or suitable plastic parts.
    • Adhesive bonding: glue wooden strips together or bond a panel to a frame.
    • Fasteners: use screws, bolts or rivets to hold parts together.
    • Joinery: assemble matching wooden joint features, such as a mortise and tenon.

    Cutting the joint features is separating; fitting and securing the parts is fabricating. In industry, “fabrication” can describe a whole production job. Here it has the narrower meaning joining.

    Conditioning changes internal properties

    Conditioning changes internal properties

    Conditioning changes how the material behaves through its structure, moisture content or chemical state. A new outline or a decorative coating is not its main goal.

    • Heat treating: use a controlled heating and cooling cycle to change properties of a suitable metal.
    • Drying or seasoning wood: reduce moisture content before later processing or service.
    • Curing: allow a resin's chemical reaction to develop its intended properties.
    • Annealing: use a controlled thermal cycle to relieve stress or change structure, as appropriate to the metal, plastic or glass.

    Conditioning can also change dimensions. Drying wood may shrink; heat treatment may distort a part. “Changes properties” does not mean “leaves every dimension unchanged.”

    Finishing treats the surface for protection or appearance

    Finishing treats the surface for protection or appearance

    Finishing changes surface condition, appearance or protection. It may add a layer, remove a little material or alter the surface itself.

    • Painting: coat a wooden panel or metal housing.
    • Plating: deposit a metal layer on a part.
    • Staining: change wood's color; stain alone does not necessarily provide a protective film.
    • Polishing: improve the surface of metal, suitable plastic or glass.

    A surface location alone does not decide the category. Surface hardening primarily changes material properties, so it belongs under conditioning in this model.

    For overlapping processes, state the purpose and pick the primary category; Practice

    For overlapping processes, state the purpose and pick the primary category

    1. Identify one operation. Break a long manufacturing description into separate actions.
    2. State its acceptance goal. What result tells you this operation is complete?
    3. Choose the category that best matches that goal. Name any secondary effect in the explanation.
    Sanding
    Sanding a block down to a specified thickness is primarily separating. Sanding out visible scratches before a clear coat is primarily finishing, although both remove material.
    Bent lamination
    Bonding thin wood layers around a curved form combines fabricating and forming. If the stated goal is the curve, call forming primary; if the question focuses on the bond between layers, call fabricating primary.
    Resin and adhesive curing
    Curing a resin part to develop properties is conditioning. Bonding two parts with that resin is primarily fabricating; curing is the property-changing step that enables the joint.
    Welding
    A weld can change nearby material properties, but a step intended to join two frame members is primarily fabricating.

    If the description only says “sanding” or “curing,” explain what purpose you are assuming. A defensible classification includes the reason.

    Practice an overlapping case Open classification practice

    Return to the six-stage material-unit map to see how these categories organize the collection.

    Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations

    Material Families

    Compare exactly four families: Metals, Plastics (polymers), Wood & Composites, and Ceramics & Glass.

    Use four material families as the starting point

    Use four material families as the starting point

    The course uses exactly four families: Metals; Plastics (polymers); Wood & Composites; Ceramics & Glass. A family helps you predict useful behavior. It does not specify a material well enough to manufacture a part.

    Classify the material in the named part, not the entire product. A kettle can have a metal body, a plastic handle and a glass window.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 19 — Why another book may show a different family list.

    Metals combine useful strength, stiffness and conductivity

    Metals combine useful strength, stiffness and conductivity

    Metals include metallic elements and alloys, mixtures designed for useful properties. Steel, aluminum and copper are everyday examples.

    Many metals conduct heat and electricity well and can deform permanently without breaking. Many are strong and stiff compared with unreinforced plastics. Density varies: aluminum is much less dense than steel, so “metal” does not always mean the heaviest choice.

    Typical matches include copper wire for electrical conduction, aluminum cookware for heat transfer, and steel fasteners for carrying loads. Corrosion behavior depends on the alloy and environment. Rust specifically concerns iron-containing materials; other metals can corrode without rusting.

    Metals may be cast, formed, cut, joined, heat treated and coated. Those process choices depend on the specific alloy and condition. Detailed metal processing belongs in the later metals topics; Milling Operations and Lathe Operations show separating operations.

    Plastics are usually light, moldable and poor conductors

    Plastics are usually light, moldable and poor conductors

    Plastics (polymers) are materials based on long molecular chains, usually with additives to adjust their behavior. Polyethylene containers, acrylic display panels and nylon gears belong here.

    Common unfilled plastics have relatively low density and low thermal and electrical conductivity. They can range from flexible to rigid, and from tough to brittle. Heat, sunlight and chemicals affect different grades differently.

    Thermoplastics can soften on heating and be reshaped under suitable conditions. Thermosets develop a chemically linked structure during curing and cannot simply be remelted into a new shape.

    “Light” does not mean “floats.” Solid acrylic is denser than water. A hollow product may float because its overall density includes the trapped air.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 20 — A supplier value that checks the floating claim.

    Wood & Composites depend on grain, layers and reinforcement

    Wood & Composites depend on grain, layers and reinforcement

    Wood has a cellular structure and grain. It is often light for its useful stiffness, relatively easy to cut and join, and a poor heat conductor. Strength and movement depend on direction and moisture content.

    A composite combines materials so they work together. Examples include plywood, wood-fiber board, glass-fiber-reinforced plastic and carbon-fiber-reinforced plastic. The material surrounding and holding reinforcement is the matrix; the reinforcement helps carry load.

    Do not assume every composite behaves like wood or like unfilled plastic. Fiber direction, layer arrangement, binder and moisture exposure affect the result. A composite can offer useful strength or stiffness for its mass while still being difficult to cut, join or repair.

    Plywood shelves and glass-fiber-reinforced boat panels belong to the same course family, but need different processing choices. Later wood topics develop grain and moisture behavior.

    Ceramics & Glass often resist heat and wear but can fracture abruptly

    Ceramics & Glass often resist heat and wear but can fracture abruptly

    Ceramics & Glass include fired clay products, porcelain, window glass and engineering ceramics such as alumina. Many are hard, resist chemical attack and carry compression well. Many also have little ability to deform permanently before fracture.

    A tile can resist scratching yet break when struck. Hardness is not toughness. Many familiar ceramics and glasses are electrical insulators, but the family contains exceptions; thermal conductivity also varies widely.

    Shaping may occur before firing, while hot, or through suitable cutting and grinding afterward. Glass can be formed while hot and annealed to reduce residual stress. Finished ceramic parts are often harder to machine than common metals or plastics.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 21 — Hard to machine does not mean impossible to machine.

    Compare typical behavior, then check the specific material; Practice

    Compare typical behavior, then check the specific material

    Use Material Properties to put a precise name to the requirement. Then select a grade, species or composite construction and check its data. No family wins on every property.

    Practice a composite classification Open material-family practice

    Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations

    Material Properties

    Distinguish strength, stiffness, hardness and toughness, then compare physical and chemical behavior, cost and workability.

    State the requirement before choosing the material

    State the requirement before choosing the material

    “Strong,” “light” and “durable” are starting points. A useful comparison says what load, temperature, environment and lifetime the part must handle.

    Mechanical properties describe behavior under force. Physical properties describe features such as density and heat or electrical behavior. Chemical properties describe interaction with the environment. Cost and workability determine whether a suitable material can become a practical product.

    Start with the four material families, then compare actual materials within them. Processing and condition matter: a material name alone does not tell you its final properties.

    Strength resists failure; stiffness limits elastic deformation

    Strength resists failure; stiffness limits elastic deformation

    Strength describes the stress a material can withstand before a specified limit, such as permanent deformation or fracture. Stress relates force to the area carrying it. A thicker part may carry more load without being made of a stronger material.

    Tensile strength
    Resistance to a pulling load. Think of a tie rod being pulled along its length.
    Compressive strength
    Resistance to a pushing or crushing load. Think of a block squeezed between two surfaces. A material good in compression may be much less capable in tension.
    Stiffness
    Resistance to elastic deformation, the change that recovers when the load is removed. A shelf that sags too far may be strong enough to avoid failure but insufficiently stiff.

    A part's stiffness depends on both its material and its geometry. Compare similarly shaped specimens when comparing materials; do not infer material stiffness by comparing a thin wire with a thick bar.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 22 — Stress, strain and modulus give the comparison units.

    Hardness, toughness, brittleness and ductility answer different questions

    Hardness, toughness, brittleness and ductility answer different questions

    Hardness
    Resistance to local indentation or scratching, depending on the test. It can help resist wear, but hardness alone does not determine wear performance.
    Toughness
    Ability to absorb energy before fracturing. A part that must survive a blow needs more than a hard surface.
    Brittleness
    A tendency to fracture with little permanent deformation. Glass may resist scratching but crack instead of bending permanently.
    Ductility
    Ability to deform permanently in tension before fracture. A ductile metal can be drawn into wire. Elastic stretch that disappears when unloaded is not the same as ductility.

    Do not treat these as synonyms. A hard ceramic tile can be brittle; a ductile metal can bend before it breaks. Toughness depends on both the stress sustained and the deformation before fracture, as well as test conditions.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 23 — Why a single “toughness number” needs its test method.

    Density and thermal behavior decide weight and temperature limits

    Density and thermal behavior decide weight and temperature limits

    Density
    Mass per unit volume. At equal volume, lower density gives lower mass. A large hollow metal part can weigh less than a small solid plastic part, so compare the whole design too.
    Melting point or melting range
    The temperature or range where a material melts. It helps choose processing conditions, but it is not the allowable service temperature: a loaded part may lose useful stiffness or strength earlier.
    Thermal conductivity
    How readily heat travels through a material. A heat spreader benefits from high conductivity; an insulating handle usually benefits from low conductivity.
    Electrical conductivity
    How readily electric current passes through a material. A wire needs a conductor; its surrounding insulation needs low conductivity under the intended conditions.

    Many common metals conduct heat and electricity well. Many unfilled plastics, dry woods and familiar ceramics are poor electrical conductors. Additives, moisture and temperature can change those tendencies.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 24 — Not every material has one useful melting-point number.

    Corrosion resistance is resistance to a particular environment

    Corrosion resistance is resistance to a particular environment

    Corrosion resistance is the ability to resist chemical or electrochemical deterioration in service. A metal that works well indoors may perform differently in salt water or against another metal.

    Rust is one form of corrosion involving iron. Aluminum and stainless steel can resist many exposures, but neither is immune to every environment. Coatings can protect a surface, and their condition matters.

    For plastics, wood and composites, also consider chemical attack, sunlight, moisture and decay as appropriate. “Does not rust” is not the same as “will last outdoors.” Name the exposure before selecting a family or grade.

    Cost and workability belong in the same comparison

    Cost and workability belong in the same comparison

    Workability means how readily a material can be processed into an acceptable part. It is specific to the operation: a material that molds well may be difficult to bond, and one that cuts readily may be unsuitable for bending.

    Cost includes more than price per mass. Consider how much material the design needs, available supply forms, tooling, processing time, waste, inspection and any protective finish.

    A family profile narrows the search: common metals often offer stiffness and conductivity; plastics often offer low mass and moldability; wood and composites offer useful directional performance; ceramics and glass often offer hardness and chemical resistance. The particular material decides whether those benefits meet the job.

    Use Manufacturing Process Categories to describe the required operations. Detailed manufacturing economics and design for manufacturing extend the cost comparison.

    Choose a candidate, give a reason, and name what still needs checking; Checklist; Practice

    Choose a candidate, give a reason, and name what still needs checking

    • Write the required function and service conditions.
    • Name the properties that control success.
    • Screen the four families, then identify a specific candidate material.
    • Check direction, temperature, moisture, processing condition and data source.
    • Check workability and total cost, then verify the finished part against its requirements.

    For a heat-spreading plate, Metals is a sensible starting family because common choices such as aluminum and copper conduct heat well. The next checks include temperature, dimensions, corrosion exposure and cost. That is a justified candidate, not a complete design specification.

    Practice selecting a family Open requirements practice

    Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations

    Additive Manufacturing Process Families

    Identify an additive process by what it places, what joins the material, and what the part still needs after the build.

    Classify the mechanism before comparing process names

    Classify the mechanism before comparing process names

    Additive manufacturing builds three-dimensional geometry by adding material. The standard process families describe how material is placed and joined. They are different from this course's five purpose categories, which describe what an operation is intended to accomplish.

    Use three questions when you meet an unfamiliar name: What feedstock enters? What places or selects each region? What joins or solidifies it? Then ask what must happen after the build before the part is ready to inspect or use.

    For the course's purpose model, additive shape-building is primarily Forming. Removing supports is a later Separating operation; curing or heat treatment can be Conditioning; finishing can change a surface. The seven AM families below do not replace those five purpose categories.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 25 — Vocabulary, brand attribution and source scope.

    Seven families place and join material in different ways

    Seven families place and join material in different ways

    FamilyFeedstock and joining mechanismA useful boundary
    Material extrusionMaterial is pushed through a nozzle and selectively deposited. A common filament route softens thermoplastic, then adjacent roads bond as they cool.FDM is a registered trademark of Stratasys; FFF is generic usage for filament fabrication. Neither name covers every extrusion feedstock.
    Vat photopolymerizationLight selectively cures liquid photopolymer held in a vat. SLA, DLP and masked exposure systems select regions differently.Cleaning, support removal and material-specific post-curing may remain. “Resin printing” does not identify one universal exposure method.
    Powder bed fusionA thin powder layer is spread, then thermal energy selectively fuses regions. Polymer SLS uses a laser; HP Multi Jet Fusion applies agents and heat. Metal routes use laser or electron-beam energy.Polymer and metal PBF share a family, not one identical workflow. Loose powder can support polymer SLS parts, while some metal routes need supports for anchoring or heat flow; process-specific exceptions exist.
    Binder jettingA printhead selectively deposits binder into a powder layer. Repeating the powder-and-binder cycle produces a fragile green shape.The printed shape is not automatically a finished dense part. Curing, depowdering, debinding, sintering or infiltration depend on the material and route.
    Material jettingDroplets containing build material are selectively deposited, then solidified or cured. PolyJet is a Stratasys photopolymer-and-UV example.The jetted liquid is build material, not merely binder placed into a powder bed. PolyJet is one branded implementation, not the family name.
    Directed energy depositionPowder or wire is delivered to a target while focused energy creates a local melt zone. Deposited tracks solidify on a substrate or existing part.The feed arrives at the deposition point rather than being spread as a complete powder layer. Repair and large features are useful contexts; finishing and inspection still matter.
    Sheet laminationSheets are bonded to build thickness, with shape developed layer by layer.The family name alone does not establish the sheet material, bonding method, accuracy or present-day machine capability.

    Material names do not move freely between families. A printer, process version and qualified feedstock must be considered together. Polymer, metal, ceramic, composite, sand and cementitious examples exist in particular systems; that does not mean every material works in every printer.

    Powder and droplets can play three different roles

    Powder and droplets can play three different roles

    Powder bed fusion
    The powder is the build material; selected regions are thermally fused during the build.
    Binder jetting
    The powder is the build material; jetted binder holds a green shape that may require later densification.
    Material jetting
    The droplets themselves contain build material; a separate support material may also be deposited in some systems.

    HP Multi Jet Fusion belongs with powder bed fusion because agents help control where powder is fused by heat. It is not binder jetting simply because a printhead deposits an agent. See the manufacturer's mechanism comparison for that distinction.

    The build is one stage of the manufacturing route; Checklist; Practice

    The build is one stage of the manufacturing route

    Judge a route from feedstock through the inspected part, not from the printer alone. Depending on the family and material, the route may include cooling, unpacking and depowdering; washing and post-curing; support removal; debinding and sintering; heat treatment; machining; surface finishing; or inspection.

    • State the material, required geometry, load direction, critical surfaces and fit.
    • Identify what carries an overhang during the build and whether that material can be removed afterward.
    • Trace trapped powder, uncured resin, support material or internal passages to an exit or cleanup method.
    • Name the state at the end of the machine cycle: finished solid, green part, supported part, powder-filled part or another intermediate state.
    • List the post-build and inspection steps required before the part can meet its intended requirement.

    No family is the universal best choice. Surface, accuracy, properties, cost and throughput depend on the actual material-process-machine combination, build use, postprocessing and acceptance requirements. Continue to FDM 3D Printing for the material-extrusion mechanism and 3D Printing from CAD for the filament CAD-to-slicer workflow.

    Identify material extrusion Distinguish fusion from binder Follow a green part

    Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations

    Powder Bed Fusion in Polymers and Metals

    Follow the shared powder-layer cycle, then distinguish polymer SLS and MJF from stated metal laser and electron-beam routes.

    Powder bed fusion repeats a spread, select, and lower cycle

    Powder bed fusion repeats a spread, select, and lower cycle

    Powder bed fusion (PBF) is one additive-manufacturing family. A machine spreads a thin powder layer, applies thermal energy to selected regions, lowers or advances the build, and repeats. Unselected powder remains around the growing parts until they are unpacked.

    The family name does not specify one material or energy source. Polymer and metal examples can share the layer cycle while differing in temperature, atmosphere, thermal behavior, support strategy, cooldown, powder recovery, postprocessing and inspection.

    Start with Additive Manufacturing Process Families for the seven-family map. PBF thermally fuses powder during the build; it is not binder jetting, where deposited binder first creates a green shape.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 26 — Readable process sources.

    Polymer SLS and MJF select powder in different ways

    Polymer SLS and MJF select powder in different ways

    Selective laser sintering (SLS)
    A laser scans selected regions of a polymer powder layer and thermally joins the particles. Unfused powder surrounds the parts in the stated process, so dedicated support structures are generally unnecessary; the build must cool before unpacking and depowdering.
    Multi Jet Fusion (MJF)
    A printhead places fusing and detailing agents on polymer powder, then applied heat fuses selected regions. The agents control fusion; they are not binder that leaves a green part for later sintering.

    Both examples belong to PBF because powder is thermally fused during the build. Neither description proves that any polymer powder, color, wall, gap or enclosed cavity will work on a particular machine.

    Loose powder can carry surrounding geometry during these stated polymer builds, but it must still be removed. A sealed hollow region can trap powder. An internal passage needs an accessible route for cleaning and inspection; “no dedicated supports” does not mean “no design constraints.”

    Metal laser and electron-beam PBF need process-specific thermal reasoning

    Metal laser and electron-beam PBF need process-specific thermal reasoning

    The metal examples here use a laser or electron beam to melt or fuse selected regions of metal powder. The part develops through repeated melt-and-solidify events, so orientation and connection to the build system can affect heat flow, residual stress, distortion and later removal.

    In a stated laser PBF case, sacrificial supports may anchor an overhang to the build plate and conduct heat away. Loose metal powder surrounding the part is not automatically an adequate thermal path. That does not create a universal rule that every metal PBF system and geometry needs the same supports.

    Electron-beam PBF has process-specific strategies and exceptions. Current commercial examples can reduce or replace traditional supports for some parts. Record the exact machine, material, melt strategy, orientation and acceptance plan instead of transferring one support rule to every metal powder process.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 27 — Why the support statement is qualified.

    Design powder access and the post-build route with the part; Checklist; Practice

    Design powder access and the post-build route with the part

    • Mark enclosed volumes, channels and lattice spaces; give loose powder a stated removal and inspection route.
    • State the material, machine/process variant, energy route and build orientation rather than writing only “PBF.”
    • Identify what supports geometry and, for the stated thermal case, what anchors the part and conducts heat.
    • Plan cooldown, unpacking, depowdering and any support removal before choosing inaccessible geometry.
    • List required postprocessing and inspection. A completed build is not automatically a qualified service part.

    Material properties and acceptance depend on the qualified material-process-part route. Use Metals and Their Properties and Plastics as Materials for material foundations; use Heat Treating Metals only when a specified metal route actually calls for that operation.

    Plan powder access Reason about a stated metal support Plan post-build acceptance

    Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Plastics

    Plastics as Materials

    Polymer chains, thermoplastics and thermosets, common plastics, and what resin identification codes actually tell you.

    Plastics get their behavior from polymer chains

    Plastics get their behavior from polymer chains

    A polymer is a substance made of very large molecules built from repeating units. Small starting molecules called monomers react to build those molecules. Many polymers have long chains; some also have branches or chemical links between chains.

    A plastic combines a polymer with ingredients that may change its color, flexibility, processing behavior or resistance to weather. The polymer name is a starting point, not a complete material specification. Two grades of the same plastic can behave differently.

    Plastics is one of the four material families in the material-family foundations topic. A polymer reinforced with glass or carbon fibers is a composite; the course places composites in Wood & Composites.

    Thermoplastics soften again; cured thermosets do not remelt

    Thermoplastics soften again; cured thermosets do not remelt

    The useful distinction is behavior on reheating
    TypeWhat happensExamples and recycling
    ThermoplasticHeating makes the material soft enough to reshape or flow. Cooling makes it firm again. Reheating can repeat this change, within the material's processing limits.PE, PP, PVC, PLA, ABS, PETG, acrylic, polycarbonate and nylon. Clean, compatible material can often be remelted for recycling; contamination, degradation and available collection systems limit actual recovery.
    ThermosetCuring forms a network of chemical links between molecules. The cured material cannot be melted back into a moldable liquid. Excessive heating degrades it.Cured epoxy and unsaturated polyester resin. They cannot be recycled by ordinary melt-and-remold processing; specialized recovery methods may exist.

    Curing is a chemical change; cooling is a temperature change. A two-part epoxy becoming solid is not simply a hot plastic cooling down.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 28 — Softening, melting and heat resistance are different questions.

    Light weight and corrosion resistance come with limits

    Light weight and corrosion resistance come with limits

    • Light weight: many unfilled plastics have much lower density than metals. Low weight does not automatically mean high stiffness.
    • Chemical resistance: plastics do not rust like steel, but a chemical may soften, swell or crack a particular plastic. Check the material, chemical, temperature and exposure time together.
    • Low softening or melting temperatures: many common thermoplastics are easy to form with heat but unsuitable for hot, loaded service.
    • Creep: slow deformation under a sustained load. A plastic shelf can keep sagging even when its load stays constant.
    • UV degradation: sunlight can discolor or embrittle susceptible grades. Outdoor service calls for a suitable resin and stabilization, not just a preferred color.
    • Electrical insulation: many unfilled plastics resist current flow. Conductive fillers and special formulations can change that behavior.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 29 — Why a short strength test does not settle a long service life.

    Match common thermoplastics to their useful properties

    Match common thermoplastics to their useful properties

    These are typical uses and tradeoffs, not design ratings for every grade. All materials in this table are thermoplastics.

    Common plastics: a first selection, followed by a grade data sheet
    MaterialTypical uses and strengthsWatch for
    PLA — polylactic acidModels, packaging and filament; stiff, often made from renewable feedstocks.Ordinary grades have limited heat resistance and can be brittle. Bio-based does not mean an item belongs in home compost or a recycling bin.
    ABS — acrylonitrile butadiene styreneHousings and toys; a useful balance of toughness and rigidity.Ordinary grades weather poorly outdoors; some solvents attack it.
    PETG — glycol-modified PETClear displays, formed packaging and filament; tough and readily thermoformed.Scratches and limited service temperature. PETG is not interchangeable with bottle-grade PET.
    Acrylic / PMMA — polymethyl methacrylateSigns, displays and glazing; clarity, stiffness and good weathering.More prone to cracking under impact than polycarbonate; vulnerable to some solvents.
    PC — polycarbonateImpact-resistant glazing and housings; transparent and tough.Scratching and chemical attack; select an appropriate UV-resistant grade for outdoor exposure.
    HDPE — high-density polyethyleneBottles, tanks and pipe; tough with useful chemical resistance.Low stiffness compared with metals, creep and substantial thermal expansion.
    LDPE — low-density polyethyleneFilm and squeeze bottles; flexible and tough.Less stiff than HDPE and limited temperature capability.
    PP — polypropyleneContainers, caps and living hinges (thin flexible connections); light and chemically resistant.Creep, UV sensitivity in unstabilized grades and reduced toughness in cold service.
    PVC — polyvinyl chlorideRigid pipe and window profiles; plasticized grades make flexible tubing and cable insulation.Properties depend strongly on additives; limited temperature range.
    Nylon / PA — polyamideGears, bearings and cable ties; strength, toughness and wear resistance.Absorbed moisture changes dimensions and mechanical properties.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 30 — Material references for checking a particular choice.

    Epoxy and polyester resin cure into thermosets

    Epoxy and polyester resin cure into thermosets

    Two common thermosetting resin systems
    ResinTypical uses and strengthsLimitations
    EpoxyAdhesives, cast parts and composite matrices; good adhesion and generally low cure shrinkage.Mixing and cure conditions affect properties. Often costs more than general-purpose polyester resin; unprotected epoxy can degrade in sunlight.
    Unsaturated polyester resinFiberglass boat shells and panels; economical for many composite parts.Typically greater cure shrinkage and lower adhesive performance than epoxy. Cured resin cannot be remelted.

    “Polyester” alone is ambiguous. PET packaging is a thermoplastic polyester. The unsaturated polyester resin used in a conventional fiberglass layup cures into a thermoset. See the hand-layup card in Plastic Forming Processes.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 31 — Where the resin comparison comes from.

    Resin codes identify plastic; they do not promise recycling; Practice

    Resin codes identify plastic; they do not promise recycling

    The number on a container is a resin identification code (RIC). It can help sorting, but it does not say whether the local recycling program accepts that product.

    The seven code-to-resin matches, checked against current public guidance
    CodePlastic
    1 — PET / PETEPolyethylene terephthalate
    2 — HDPEHigh-density polyethylene
    3 — PVCPolyvinyl chloride (vinyl)
    4 — LDPELow-density polyethylene
    5 — PPPolypropylene
    6 — PSPolystyrene
    7 — OTHERResins outside the first six categories; also some combinations of resins. It is not one particular plastic.

    For example, code 5 identifies PP; it does not prove that a PP lid is accepted with PP containers. Use the collector's instructions for that item. Do not assign PETG to code 1 just because its name contains PET.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 32 — Verified code sources and the standard's exact distinction.
