    Critical Dimensions for the Shop

    Choose dimensions from fit, function and interfaces, then give the maker and inspector the same references and limits.

    A critical dimension controls fit, function or an interface

    A critical dimension controls fit, function or an interface

    A critical dimension is one whose variation can stop the part doing its job. Start with what touches another part, what must move or clear, and what locates the part. A hole's diameter may control whether a pin enters; its position may control whether two parts line up.

    Critical does not mean “make every tolerance tight.” A tolerance is the permitted variation in a dimension. Choose it from the function, then check that the process and inspection method can achieve it. See Tolerances and Fits for limits and fits, Measurement Language for units and measurement language, and Surface Texture and Finish for surface requirements.

    Give hole locations from named reference edges

    Give hole locations from named reference edges

    The original DL-01 display plate below illustrates a shop drawing. Its two suspension holes must stay at the intended locations; length and width mainly establish the display area. These are invented teaching limits, not a general specification for plywood or hanging hardware.

    DL-01 revision A — drawing requirements
    FeatureRequirementReason / inspection
    Material and outlineBirch plywood; length 100 ±1; width 40 ±1; thickness 6 ±0.5 mm.Display area and thickness. Measure with calipers; check adjacent edges with a try square for no visible gap.
    C — two through holesEach diameter 4.5 ±0.2 mm.Openings for the loops; use suitable plug gauges for 4.3–4.7 mm limits.
    C — center positionsFrom L: x = 15 ±0.5 and 85 ±0.5 mm. From B: y = 20 ±0.5 mm for each.Consistent suspension locations. Check each coordinate from the stated edge.
    Surface and edgesNo coating; no loose fibers, splits or separated plywood layers.Visual inspection after sanding; retain the dimensional limits.

    All features have requirements, including those not marked C. See Operation Method Sheets for the manufacturing sequence and Bills of Materials for the matching parts list.

    Worked record: correct horizontal separation, wrong locations

    For this classroom comparison with DL-01 revision A, treat the following readings as exact mm values. The near-edge readings run horizontally right from L and vertically up from B to the nearest edge of each hole. Calculate each center using that hole's measured diameter.

    • Left hole: diameter 4.6; near edges 13.3 from L and 17.2 from B. Center x = 13.3 + 4.6/2 = 15.6 mm; y = 17.2 + 4.6/2 = 19.5 mm.
    • Right hole: diameter 4.4; near edges 83.4 from L and 18.3 from B. Center x = 83.4 + 4.4/2 = 85.6 mm; y = 18.3 + 4.4/2 = 20.5 mm.

    Record the comparisons: both diameters meet 4.3–4.7 mm. Left x = 15.6 exceeds 15.5; right x = 85.6 exceeds 85.5, so both x locations fail. Both y locations meet 19.5–20.5 mm, including its endpoints. The horizontal separation is 85.6 − 15.6 = 70.0 mm, the nominal x-coordinate difference, but the pair is shifted right. These hole readings do not meet the drawing's separate location limits; correct horizontal separation alone does not locate the pair. This record compares only the stated hole readings, not the outline, thickness or surface requirements.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 93 — How to check a center when a caliper touches the hole edge.

    Dimension the part so it can be made without measuring the picture; Checklist; Practice

    Dimension the part so it can be made without measuring the picture

    Include the part identity, revision, material, units, overall dimensions, feature sizes and locations, thickness, and required finish. Supply enough views to remove ambiguity. Call a hole “through” when it passes through the material; otherwise specify depth.

    Locate related features from a common reference where that matches their function. Do not give multiple independent dimensions for the same feature unless their relationship is clear. A redundant dimension can contradict the dimensions used to make the part.

    • Identify every mating surface, clearance and locating feature.
    • Choose references the maker can establish and the inspector can reach.
    • Check that each feature has a size, location and acceptance limit.
    • Remove conflicting or missing dimensions; do not rely on drawing scale.
    • Match the drawing revision to the method sheet and BOM.

    Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Manufacturing Documentation

    Bills of Materials

    List the parts in an assembly and estimate each part's material share without confusing stock purchases with per-part consumption.

    A bill of materials says what goes into one assembly

    A bill of materials says what goes into one assembly

    A bill of materials (BOM) lists the parts needed for a product. Give each part a stable number, a clear name, a quantity per assembly, a material and a make-or-buy designation. Identify the stock for made parts and the purchasing description for bought parts.

    Made means the part needs a drawing and a route such as an operation method sheet. Bought means it arrives as a component; it still needs a size and specification so the buyer can obtain the correct item. Match the BOM revision to the assembly drawing. State whether quantities are per assembly or for the whole batch.

    Material cost per part is its allocated stock share times stock price

    Material cost per part is its allocated stock share times stock price

    Estimated material cost per part = stock share allocated to that part × price of that stock unit. Keep both amounts on the same basis: length for constant-section bar, area for sheet of the same thickness, or mass when purchased by mass.

    Allow for the saw cut's width (kerf), trimming and unusable stock. Finished-part volume alone can understate what making the part consumes. State how you allocate waste and reusable leftovers so two estimates can be compared.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 94 — Consumption, purchase cost and batch yield answer different questions.

    Worked BOM: one display label assembly costs $1.20 in allocated materials

    Worked BOM: one display label assembly costs $1.20 in allocated materials

    This original example matches DL-01 in Operation Method Sheets and Critical Dimensions for the Shop. All prices are invented teaching values, not quotations. Assembly DL-A, revision A, contains one made plywood plate and two purchased closed cord loops.

    The 110 × 50 × 6 mm starting blank is allocated a 120 × 60 mm area of a 1200 × 120 × 6 mm birch plywood strip costing $18. The larger allocation includes room for cutting and trimming. Allocation share = (120 × 60) / (1200 × 120) = 0.05. Plate material estimate = 0.05 × $18 = $0.90.

    DL-A revision A — quantities and material estimate per assembly
    Part number / nameMake / buy; material and stockQuantityCost eachExtended cost
    DL-01 / display label plateMake; birch plywood, blank 110 × 50 × 6 mm; allocated stock area 120 × 60 mm as above.1$0.90$0.90
    DL-02 / closed cord loopBuy; waxed cotton cord, 1 mm diameter, 100 mm closed-loop circumference; example pack of 20 for $3.2$0.15$0.30
    Total allocated material and purchased-component cost per assembly$1.20

    Extended cost is quantity × cost each. The $1.20 excludes labor, machine time, tooling, consumables, taxes and delivery. It is not a complete manufacturing cost or a selling price. Broader cost roll-up and design-for-manufacturing decisions belong with manufacturing economics.

    Buying one strip and one pack costs $21, even for one assembly. Unused material remains inventory; do not confuse that purchase total with $1.20 of allocated consumption.

    Check quantities, units and waste before totaling the BOM; Checklist; Practice

    Check quantities, units and waste before totaling the BOM

    • Match every drawing part number to a BOM row.
    • State the quantity per assembly and multiply once for the batch quantity.
    • Specify stock dimensions and material for made parts, and purchasing details for bought parts.
    • Use the same units in the stock-share numerator and denominator.
    • Document the cutting allowance and treatment of leftovers.
    • Multiply each quantity by its unit cost and sum the extended costs.

    Keep unrounded intermediate calculations; round money to cents at the stated reporting step.

    Operation Method Sheets

    Turn a drawing into an ordered plan with equipment, setup, process settings and a check that proves each operation is complete.

    A method sheet tells another person how to make and check the part

    A method sheet tells another person how to make and check the part

    A drawing describes the required part. An operation method sheet describes how to make it. A process plan or routing sheet serves the same planning purpose, although the amount of detail varies. Write one row for each operation, in the order it will be performed.

    Start with the part number and name, drawing revision, date, material and raw stock size: the starting piece before machining or cutting. Use actual dimensions and units. A material family alone is not a purchasing specification; identify the material needed for this part.

    What belongs in each operation row
    FieldWhat the next person needs
    OperationAn action and its intended result, such as drill two through holes.
    Equipment and setup/toolingThe equipment, cutting tool, support, holding method and reference face or edge.
    Process parametersSettings with units, or an identified approved setup instruction. Do not write an unexplained number for speed or feed.
    Setup and cycle timeTime to prepare the operation, separate from time to repeat it on one part.
    Pass/fail criteria and inspection toolsThe required result, permitted limits and how to measure or compare it.

    Keep quality checkpoints, failed-part decisions, actual times and improvement notes with the sheet. Equipment permission and operating procedures still come from Equipment Operating Procedure; a method sheet is not machine training.

    Establish reference surfaces before locating features

    Establish reference surfaces before locating features

    Choose the order around what each later step needs. Make a straight, square reference edge before measuring hole locations from it. Make features while there is enough material to support and hold the work. Inspect a feature before the next step hides it.

    Holes may be easier to make before small parts are cut free from a larger piece. Final finishing usually follows cutting and drilling, so those operations do not damage the finished surface. Inspect afterward too: finishing can change dimensions.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 95 — Why there is no universal operation order.

    Worked method sheet: a hanging display label

    Worked method sheet: a hanging display label

Finished dimensions and acceptance limits are on the example drawing. Two purchased cord loops complete the assembly in Bills of Materials. No coating is specified.

    For three assemblies, the serial estimate is 10 + (3 × 13) = 49 minutes, assuming each setup is done once and all operations run one after another. Record waiting, interruptions and repeated setups separately when comparing with actual elapsed time.

    Replace “make it right” with an action and an acceptance test; Checklist; Practice

    Replace “make it right” with an action and an acceptance test

    “Drill the holes neatly” leaves the next person guessing. “Drill two through holes at the drawing coordinates; check diameter and location against revision A” gives an action and a result, but still needs the equipment, support, tooling and settings in the row.

    Pass means every stated criterion is met. Fail means identify and hold the part for a decision; do not quietly send it to the next operation. Rework is a specified additional operation that can bring the part into conformance. Removing more material cannot restore an undersize outside dimension or shrink an oversize hole.

    • Match the part, drawing and method-sheet revisions.
    • Check that every operation names equipment, tooling, holding and references.
    • Fill required settings with units before releasing the plan.
    • Give every quality checkpoint a measurable limit or an explicit comparison and an inspection method.
    • Define who decides rework or rejection when a check fails.

    Record what changed so the next batch can repeat the improvement

    Record what changed so the next batch can repeat the improvement

    Record setup time once per setup and cycle time per piece. State when each timer starts and stops; include inspection consistently. Keep quantity attempted, quantity accepted, scrap count and rework count. A reworked part may later pass, so these counts are not all separate groups to add together.

    For each trial, record material identity, tool, setting and units, holding arrangement, actual measurements and the problem observed. A useful photo shows the reference edge, stop or tool position; caption it with the operation and revision. Use photos you have permission to share, with no personal information.

    Example improvement record — a proposed trial, not a claimed result
    ObservationChange to testEvidence to keep
    Hole locations vary between pieces.Use the same reference edges and a verified locating stop instead of re-marking from different edges.Record each hole location before and after the change, batch size, setup time and rejects. Keep the acceptance limits unchanged.

    Change one factor at a time where practical. Verify the first piece after a setup change before repeating it through a batch. If the change helps, update the method-sheet revision and keep the evidence. A faster operation that produces more rejects is not automatically an improvement.

    Making Silicone Molds from a Printed Pattern

    Plan a one-part mold, document the product-specific mixing and curing conditions, and inspect a repeatable batch of castings.

    A printed pattern defines the cavity in the silicone mold; Interactive; Practice

    A printed pattern defines the cavity in the silicone mold

    A pattern is the original shape copied by a mold. For a simple one-part, open-face mold, use a shape with a flat back and features that can be withdrawn through the opening. An original example is a small decorative relief tile with a flat back, gently sloping sides and no hooked details.

    For a small batch of resin replicas, this is a casting task: liquid resin fills the mold cavity and cures. A fiber-reinforced shell made by wet hand layup builds layers of reinforcing fabric or mat with resin against a mold. Compare these routes in Plastic Forming Processes, then use Choosing a Plastic Forming Process to weigh material, geometry, quantity and tooling. Try the detailed-replica and reinforced-shell practice choices.

    Draft is a slight taper that helps a part leave the mold. Let the shape widen toward the opening. A flat parting face, where the pattern meets the mold-box base, defines the open back of this mold. Avoid undercuts that hook behind the silicone; flexibility does not make every trapped shape removable.

    A wide mouth does not rule out an interior hook. This illustrative model uses an exact-fit, centered, symmetric rigid 2D pattern and rigid cavity. Opening depth is 0; positive depth points down into the mold. The only permitted motion is outward translation upward at fixed orientation, into unobstructed space. Units are arbitrary consistent diagram units.

    Exact piecewise-linear sections: stations are (depth, half-width)
    ProfileStationsTrial pull 5Whole path
    Taper(0,30), (40,20)1.25 side separationNo positive interference
    Parallel(0,25), (40,25)Side contactNo positive interference; contact persists
    Reverse taper(0,20), (40,30)1.25 interference per sideBlocked
    Local shoulder(0,30), (20,22), (25,26), (40,15)Maximum 4 interference per side at depth 20Blocked despite widest mouth

    At cavity depth d, an outward pull t places pattern half-width w(d+t) against cavity half-width w(d). Positive Δ(d) = w(d+t) − w(d) means overlap. For the local shoulder at t = 5, the positive interval is (50/3, 520/23), approximately (16.6667, 22.6087); endpoints are zero-contact boundaries.

    The continuous path requires width to be nonincreasing with depth. A deeper section wider than a shallower section provides an obstruction. For each pose, Δ is linear between original and translated knots; checking these knots and solving zero crossings is analytical, not an animation-frame test. At t = 0 every profile is in initial contact. At t = 40 there is no interior overlap, but the reverse taper and local shoulder still have blocked paths: a clear endpoint does not prove a reachable endpoint.

    Comparisons use a numerical threshold of 64 × machine epsilon × maximum half-width, separate from physical clearance and manufacturing tolerance. Values within that floating-point threshold are treated as contact. This is geometric interference only: it omits friction, adhesion, shrinkage, forces, damage, cure, rotation, lateral motion, deformation and unshown 3D features. No-interference does not establish practical release; a rigid obstruction does not establish flexible-silicone failure.

    Remove unwanted layer ridges and support marks without losing important dimensions. Choose pattern preparation, any sealer and any release agent for the specific print, silicone and casting material. Follow the manufacturers' compatibility instructions and test a small prepared sample before committing the full mold.

    Read the technical data sheet before choosing a mix or cure schedule; Checklist

    Read the technical data sheet before choosing a mix or cure schedule

    The technical data sheet (TDS) supplies processing instructions. The safety data sheet (SDS) supplies handling information; use Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets for that guidance. Neither a generic lesson nor a familiar-looking container replaces the instructions for the actual product.

    • Record the silicone product, batch identification and technical-sheet revision.
    • Record the A:B ratio and whether it is by mass (weight) or by volume.
    • Record working time, mixing procedure, bubble-removal requirements and cure conditions.
    • Check compatibility with the printed pattern, coatings, release agent and intended casting material.
    • Complete a small compatibility trial and inspect its cure before the full pour.

    Working time is the available time to mix and place the material under stated conditions. It is not the demolding time. Cure instructions may distinguish demolding from full properties or further treatment. Record the actual temperature and times; do not substitute a universal overnight wait.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 96 — Where to find product-specific instructions.

    A ratio by weight is not automatically a ratio by volume; Interactive; Practice

    A ratio by weight is not automatically a ratio by volume

    Read what the given mass represents. These invented A/B examples teach arithmetic for two-component materials; they are not silicone or resin recipes. For A:B = a:b by mass and target total material mass M, mA = M a/(a+b) and mB = M b/(a+b). If A is already measured, mB = mA b/a.

    Same 10:1 mass specification, different meaning of 220 g
    GivenABMaterial total
    220 g target total200 g20 g220 g
    220 g of A alone220 g22 g242 g

    Density connects mass and each component’s own volume: VA = mA/ρA and VB = mB/ρB. For a:b by volume, divide target total mass using weights aρA:bρB. For given A mass, VA = mA/ρA, VB = VA b/a, then mB = VBρB.

    Use illustrative densities ρA = 1.2 g/mL and ρB = 0.8 g/mL with a 300 g target total:

    Changing the basis while keeping 2:1 changes the specification
    A:B specificationA mass / volumeB mass / volume
    2:1 by mass200 g / 500/3 mL (≈166.6667 mL)100 g / 125 mL
    2:1 by volume225 g / 187.5 mL75 g / 93.75 mL

    The first row has a 4:3 component-volume ratio; the second has a 3:1 mass ratio. Those are equivalent descriptions of their respective batches. Converting 300 g to 0.3 kg keeps the same physical batch. Switching 2:1 from mass to volume does not. Individual component volumes do not establish mixed/cured volume, yield or cavity fill.

    Ideal cumulative scale example: for 200 g A + 20 g B in a 35 g container, readings with no tare are 35 g empty → 235 g after A → 255 g after B. Tare once with the empty container on the scale and the readings are 0 g → 200 g → 220 g. The final reading includes A and B; B alone is 20 g. Container mass changes the gross reading, not the material ratio. This comparison does not re-tare after A.

    Weigh with a scale suitable for the actual quantities and follow the product’s specified ratio basis, measurement and mixing procedure. The arithmetic assumes no material loss; it predicts no cure, exotherm, working time, compatibility or actual mixed/cured volume. The actual product’s TDS/SDS remain authoritative.

    Practice a total-mass mix Practice a given-A mix

    Document pattern preparation, pouring and cure as separate operations

    Document pattern preparation, pouring and cure as separate operations

    1. Prepare the pattern and box. Inspect the print, complete the qualified surface treatment, secure its flat back to the box base, and check that the box contains the liquid. Set wall and backing thickness from the mold material and geometry requirements.
    2. Measure and mix. Record actual A and B quantities, the ratio basis and the start time. Follow the product's mixing instructions, including its directions for reaching material at the container walls and bottom.
    3. Reduce trapped air. Follow the product's bubble-removal and pouring instructions. A controlled pour into a low point can let the material rise around the pattern instead of repeatedly trapping air over its details. Vacuum degassing is product- and equipment-dependent; do not assume every silicone requires it or has enough working time for it.
    4. Cure and remove the pattern. Record temperature, elapsed time and the specified demolding condition. Inspect the mold surface and details after removal before using the cavity.
    5. Make a first casting. Follow the casting material's own mixing, release and cure instructions. Its ratio and timing need not match the silicone's. Inspect the first piece before repeating the batch.

    Use Operation Method Sheets to give each operation equipment, settings, timing and a pass/fail check. Record what actually happened, including a changed pour method or a delayed demold, rather than copying the planned values into the result column.

    Inspect each casting for voids, dimensions and consistency

    Inspect each casting for voids, dimensions and consistency

    A void is an unintended empty region. Inspect visible faces, edges and small details for pits, missing material and incomplete filling. A good exterior does not prove that the interior has no voids; choose further inspection according to the part's function.

    Define batch checks before casting
    CheckWhat to document
    Shape and dimensionsDrawing limits, measurement method and actual readings for critical features.
    Visible surfaceWhich faces matter and what counts as a reject. For a teaching relief tile, an example criterion is no visible pits or missing raised detail on the display face.
    Cure and releaseProduct-specific acceptance condition; any tacky region, tearing or distortion observed on removal.
    Batch consistencyCasting number, material batch, measured charge, mixing and cure times, appearance, dimensions, rejects and rework.

    If a defect repeats at the same position, inspect the corresponding mold feature. If it varies between pours, compare the recorded process conditions. These are starting points for investigation, not proof of a cause. Change one factor, make a trial, and retain the results before revising the approved method.

    Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations

    Manufacturing Cost and Volume

    Estimate unit cost and find where two production methods cost the same.

    Count material, processing, quality and overhead costs once

    Count material, processing, quality and overhead costs once

    Material, labor, machine time, tooling and scrap all affect the cost of an acceptable part. Setup prepares an operation; cycle time is the time for a repeating operation.

    • Material: stock purchase, delivery and material lost during production.
    • Processing: labor, machine time, tools, consumables and energy.
    • Quality: prevention, inspection, rework, rejects and returns.
    • Overhead: shared support such as facilities and indirect labor.

    Check what a machine rate already includes before adding labor, energy or depreciation. Scrap belongs in the estimate once, even if it appears under both material and quality headings.

    Spread fixed cost over the quantity actually needed; Practice

    Spread fixed cost over the quantity actually needed

    For a simple batch model, C = F + vQ and u = C/Q = F/Q + v. C is total cost, F is fixed batch cost, v is variable cost per part, Q is the number of acceptable parts, and u is average unit cost. Use Q greater than zero.

    Fixed cost stays constant within the stated production range; variable cost grows with quantity. Setup and dedicated tooling may be fixed for a batch. Material and processing per part often contribute to v. State the period and cost boundary before classifying a cost.

    Illustrative process A costs $120 + $8Q. At 60 parts, total cost is $600 and unit cost is $10.00/part. Producing unwanted parts to spread fixed cost creates inventory; it does not create demand.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 97 — Why a shorter cycle does not reduce every cost equally.

    Practice unit cost

    Set total costs equal to find process break-even; Practice

    Set total costs equal to find process break-even

    Compare routes that meet the same requirements at the same quantity. From F_A + v_A Q = F_B + v_B Q, obtain Q* = (F_B − F_A)/(v_A − v_B).

    Let A cost $120 + $8Q and B cost $720 + $3Q. Then Q* = ($720 − $120)/($8 − $3) = 120 parts. Both cost $1,080 total or $9/part. A costs less below 120; B costs less above 120.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 98 — When there is no positive crossing.

    Practice break-even

    Move the volume slider and predict which process wins; Interactive

    Move the volume slider and predict which process wins

    Start with the original A/B costs and predict the cheaper process at 60 and 240 parts. Then change a setup cost or variable cost and compare at the same demanded quantity. The case selector also includes fractional crossings, parallel lines, an everywhere tie, and a crossing beyond the chart.

    Process-cost explorer. Compare C = F + vQ and u = F/Q + v for two routes supplying the same demanded quantity of equivalent acceptable parts in one batch. Use the same included costs and period for each route, count each cost once, and assume the entered rates stay constant. The exercise does not establish equivalent quality, capacity or demand, or recommend a purchase.

    Predict, calculate total cost for each route, then divide by the demanded quantity. With A = $120 + $8Q and B = $720 + $3Q:

    Original comparison at three demanded quantities
    PartsA total / per partB total / per partLower cost
    60$600 / $10.00$900 / $15.00A
    120$1,080 / $9.00$1,080 / $9.00Equal
    240$2,040 / $8.50$1,440 / $6.00B

    Between whole parts: let A = $90 + $6Q and B = $245 + $2Q. Q* = 155/4 = 38.75 parts. At 38 parts A totals $318 and B $321; at 39 parts A totals $324 and B $323. No whole-part quantity ties.

    Try the other cases: A = $60 + $4Q and B = $210 + $4Q never cross because their slopes match; A stays $150 lower. If both F and v match, costs tie at every positive quantity. With A = $80 + $2Q and B = $200 + $5Q, A is lower for every positive Q. With A = $100 + $2.50Q and B = $900 + $2Q, the positive crossing is at 1,600 parts, beyond the live graph's 0–300 interval.

    The editable explorer accepts fixed cost $0–$100,000, variable cost $0–$1,000/part and whole demand 1–10,000. Dollar entries have at most two decimal places; exact cent totals determine equality. Displayed average unit costs are approximate. A graph ending before a crossing does not prove there is no crossing. Zero on a total-cost graph shows fixed cost; unit cost at zero parts is undefined.

    Static comparison: at 60 parts A is $10.00/part and B is $15.00/part; at 240 parts A is $8.50/part and B is $6.00/part. Use Dimensional Analysis to check units and Outsourcing to consider more than cost.

    Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations

    Material Utilization and Cost

    Check a stock layout, account for cutting loss and roll up material costs.

    Prove the parts fit before dividing areas; Practice

    Prove the parts fit before dividing areas

    Stock is material purchased for further work. Nesting arranges part outlines on stock to reduce waste. An area ratio cannot prove a layout fits. Check dimensions, orientation, grain direction where relevant, edge margins and spacing.

    Kerf is the width removed by a cut. An offcut is leftover stock; a usable offcut may be saved. Include trim cuts and holding allowances before promising a part count.

    Illustrative layout: a 1,000 mm bar supplies 98 mm blanks. Each blank requires one 2 mm separating cut, including the last blank, with no end trim. Ten blanks consume 10 × (98 + 2) = 1,000 mm. A different last-cut arrangement would need a different cut count.

    Practice kerf allowance

    Test the next-blank threshold; Interactive; Practice

    Test the next-blank threshold

    Predict first: can the same 1,000 mm stock still supply ten 98 mm blanks if separating kerf increases from 2 to 3 mm? What happens to stock cost per blank when the stock price stays $48?

    This one-dimensional lab reserves a full separating kerf after every blank, including the last. Left and right excluded trim lengths already include their own cut losses. The layout does not use the far stock edge as a finished blank edge; it is a count under this policy, not a claim of globally maximum yield.

    Usable interval U = stock length L − left excluded trim − right excluded trim
    Blank count n = floor[U / (blank length b + separating kerf k)]. Round down to a whole number. There are n separating cuts, plus any preparation already accounted for in excluded trim.

    Each outlined block is an actual 98 mm blank; the narrow filled band after each is its full 2 mm kerf. Ten blanks plus ten kerfs fill this stock exactly. On narrow screens, scroll sideways to inspect the full bar.

    Material balance: 1,000 mm = 0 excluded trim + 980 acceptable blanks + 20 separating kerfs + 0 offcut. Utilization = 980 / 1,000 × 100 = 98.0%.

    Change the kerf to 3 mm: ten blanks would need 10 × (98 + 3) = 1,010 mm, so only nine fit. The new balance is 1,000 = 0 + 882 + 27 + 91 mm. The 91 mm offcut is 10 mm short of another 101 mm blank-and-kerf interval.

    Allocate the whole stock charge: $48 / 10 = $4.80 per acceptable blank in the original layout; $48 / 9 ≈ $5.33 after the kerf change. All equal-cross-section blanks are assumed acceptable. No remnant credit or processing cost is included. If zero blanks fit, cost per blank is undefined.

    Another threshold: at 2 mm kerf, 999.99 mm stock fits nine blanks, while 1,000.00 mm fits ten. This lab uses hundredths of a millimeter and currency cents; its bounded illustrative values are not machine settings. It is not a two-dimensional nesting tool.

    Practice stock layout and balance Practice a count threshold

    Use a consistent physical basis for utilization; Practice

    Use a consistent physical basis for utilization

    Utilization = material in acceptable parts / material purchased × 100%. Compare length for the same cross-section, area for the same thickness, or mass on a consistent basis.

    The bar example gives 980/1,000 × 100 = 98.0%. The remaining 2% is kerf. Distinguish reusable offcuts from material discarded.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 99 — Why 20% loss means a 25% increase per useful amount.

    Practice utilization

    Charge each part its share of stock and waste; Practice

    Charge each part its share of stock and waste

    Part material cost = share of stock charged to the part × stock price. A $48 sheet yielding eight identical acceptable blanks gives $48 × 1/8 = $6.00 per blank when the whole sheet is charged to those blanks. This includes their share of kerf and unusable offcuts.

    Finished-part area divided by stock area can understate cost by leaving waste unassigned. State any credit for reusable remnants. Add delivery only if it is not already in the stock price.

    Practice stock cost

    Multiply quantity by unit cost for each BOM line

    Multiply quantity by unit cost for each BOM line

    A bill of materials (BOM) lists the components and quantities needed for one product. Add quantity × unit cost for every line.

    Illustrative material-only BOM
    ItemQuantityUnit costLine cost
    Blank2$6.00$12.00
    Standard fastener4$0.25$1.00
    Material total$13.00

    This is not finished product cost. Add processing, assembly and other applicable costs using Manufacturing Cost and Volume.

    Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations

    Outsourcing

    Decide which activities to keep in-house or place with suppliers, weighing relevant costs and capabilities alongside quality, capacity and delivery.

    Compare equivalent acceptable parts over the same period

    Compare equivalent acceptable parts over the same period

    Outsourcing means arranging for an outside supplier to carry out work for the business rather than doing it internally. The work may be making a component or providing a service. A make-or-buy comparison is one application of that broader decision.

    A core competence is a capability central to what the business does particularly well. Outsourcing may free resources to focus on those strengths, but it also makes the business depend on suppliers for the work they perform. Compare costs alongside capacity, quality, delivery and capabilities worth retaining. See OpenStax: Outsourcing and core strengths.

    Make means produce internally; buy means purchase from a supplier. Define quantity, specifications and delivery date before comparing options. Use Manufacturing Cost and Volume for an initial cost comparison.

    Include avoidable setup, tooling, material and processing for make; purchase price, freight, incoming checks and expected rework for buy. Compare costs that change with the decision. Shared rent that remains after outsourcing is not automatically a cash saving.

    Start here: decide which future costs change between the two routes, then compare their totals. A relevant cost changes with the choice. An avoidable cost is removed by choosing the other route; a sunk cost has already been incurred and cannot be recovered. Fixed, direct and allocated describe costs, but those labels alone do not establish relevance.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 100 — Why the cost boundary matters.

    Worked case: which costs change for 100 parts?; Practice

    Worked case: which costs change for 100 parts?

    This original hypothetical order needs 100 acceptable brackets delivered within one month. All amounts below are illustrative dollars, not supplier prices or facts about a particular shop. For the numeric comparison, assume both routes supply the same specification and acceptable quantity by that deadline.

    Making needs a new $300 setup and $9 per acceptable part ($6 material plus $3 additional processing). Buying needs a $10 per-part quote, a separate $0.50 incoming check per part, and $100 freight for the order. The quote excludes those checks and freight. These are future payments incurred only for their respective routes.

    The $600 shared rent for the month is paid unchanged either way. A $200 study was paid for last month and is irrecoverable. Assume spare internal capacity, no displaced work or alternative income, and no other route-dependent costs or credits. These are case assumptions; spare time alone does not establish that opportunity cost is zero in a real decision.

    Predict before reading the totals: does making's lower per-part charge outweigh its new setup at this quantity? Which two amounts should be excluded from the relevant-cost totals?

    Relevant-cost ledger — the same 100 acceptable parts and one-month boundary
    Cost and treatmentMakeBuy
    New setup: avoidable if buying$300$0
    Material + additional processing: $9 × 100$900$0
    Supplier quote: $10 × 100$0$1,000
    Separate incoming checks: $0.50 × 100$0$50
    Freight: once per order$0$100
    Shared rent: $600 either way, excluded——
    Past study: $200 irrecoverable, excluded——
    Total relevant cost$1,200$1,150

    Here “—” means excluded from this comparison, not a zero expense. Make = $300 + $900 = $1,200; buy = $1,000 + $50 + $100 = $1,150. Buying is $50 lower under the stated assumptions. The new setup matters even though it is fixed for this order: buying avoids it. Adding the unchanged rent to both sides would leave the $50 difference unchanged; adding it only to make would invent a saving.

    For a quantity sensitivity check, use the existing Manufacturing Cost and Volume explorer with A as make ($300 setup, $9/part) and B as buy ($100 order freight, $10.50/part). Identify relevant costs first; the explorer cannot decide which costs belong. Do not add freight or checks again after including them in those inputs.

    Practice: include the avoidable setup Practice: count buying charges once

    A cheaper quote can still be the wrong choice; Practice

    A cheaper quote can still be the wrong choice

    FactorQuestion
    CapacityIs machine and staff time available? What other useful work would be displaced?
    QualityCan each route meet the specification consistently, and how will it be verified?
    Lead timeCan the route deliver when needed, including queues and transport?
    Core competenceIs this capability central to what the organization does well and needs to retain?
    RiskWhat happens if demand changes, a supplier fails or the design changes?

    Standard parts often favor buying; distinctive capabilities may favor making. Neither is a rule based on volume alone.

    The worked case establishes a conditional cost difference. It does not verify a supplier's quality, available capacity or delivery promise. Before committing, obtain evidence that each route can meet the requirement. If making displaces another useful job, include the benefit given up; if buying adds rework, expediting or other costs, revise the ledger. See OpenStax: Make or buy a component for avoidable fixed costs and the qualitative checks alongside the numeric analysis.

    Practice: what does the result support?

    Check assumptions before committing resources; Checklist; Practice

    Check assumptions before committing resources

    • Define matching requirements, quantity and timing.
    • List relevant costs and identify charges already included in rates.
    • Check capacity, quality evidence, lead time and supplier dependence.
    • Repeat the comparison at lower and higher plausible demand.
    • Record what would change the decision.

    Review Design for Manufacturing before treating a costly design as fixed.

    Practice: separate unchanged and sunk costs

    Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations

    Design for Manufacturing

    Make the required function easier to produce, assemble, inspect and maintain.

    Keep the function and simplify how it is made

    Keep the function and simplify how it is made

    Design for manufacturing (DFM) considers production while a design can still change. Preserve required strength, fit and service performance; remove complexity that serves no requirement.

    • Reduce separate parts when this simplifies production and service.
    • Use standard components and available stock sizes.
    • Match geometry to the process and provide tool and inspection access.
    • Make assembly easy to orient, reach and verify.

    Fewer parts can reduce joining work, but one complex part may need costly tooling or be hard to repair. Compare the whole route.

    Specify only the precision the function needs

    Specify only the precision the function needs

    A tolerance is the allowed variation in a dimension or other feature. Tight tolerances may require careful setups, slower processing and more capable inspection. Keep tight control where fit or function needs it; do not apply it everywhere by habit.

    No machine name guarantees a tolerance or price. Geometry, material, tooling, setup and measurement all matter. Confirm capability for the actual feature.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 101 — Why the loosest tolerance is not automatically cheapest.

    Reduce material loss without shortening useful life; Checklist

    Reduce material loss without shortening useful life

    Use Material Utilization and Cost to compare layouts. Also consider energy, durability, repair, disassembly and practical material recovery at end of life. A lighter part that fails early may consume more resources over its service life.

    • Identify each part's function and critical features.
    • Check standard components and stock sizes.
    • Sketch manufacturing, assembly and inspection access.
    • Check tolerances against function and process capability.
    • Compare material use, service life and repair or recycling options.
    Lean and Quality/Continuous Improvement

    Lean Value and Flow

    Define customer value and improve the whole path from request to delivery.

    Start with what the customer needs

    Start with what the customer needs

    Lean thinking improves how work creates value while reducing waste and respecting the people doing it. Value is judged from the customer's need: the right function and quality, in the needed quantity, at the needed time.

    A busy machine is not proof of useful output. Making something early that nobody needs can increase storage and delay the work that is needed.

    Separate value creation from necessary support and avoidable waste

    Separate value creation from necessary support and avoidable waste

    Value-added work changes the product or service toward the customer's requirement and is done correctly. Cutting a needed feature may add value; searching for a misplaced tool does not.

    Some non-value-added work is currently necessary: required checks, safety measures and records protect customers and workers. Improve how that work is done; do not delete a safeguard because it does not physically change the product.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 102 — Process time is not automatically value-added time.

    Follow the work across handoffs

    Follow the work across handoffs

    Improving one station can build a queue at the next. Look at the whole path with Value Stream Mapping. Use Eight Wastes: TIMWOODS to describe problems and Kaizen and Standard Work to test improvements with the people doing the work.

    5S Workplace Organization supports visible, repeatable work. It is one supporting method, not the whole of lean.

    Lean and Quality/Continuous Improvement

    Eight Wastes: TIMWOODS

    Recognize eight patterns of wasted effort in manufacturing and daily life.

    Use TIMWOODS to name what you observe

    Use TIMWOODS to name what you observe

    Transportation, Inventory, Motion, Waiting, Overproduction, Over-processing, Defects and Skills form TIMWOODS. Describe the observed problem before choosing a remedy.

    Compare shop examples with everyday examples

    Compare shop examples with everyday examples

    These are illustrative examples, not descriptions of a particular shop.

    Transportation: unnecessary material movement

    Shop: A part travels to a distant holding area and back.
    Daily life: Moving stored boxes between rooms without using them.

    Inventory: excess material or work

    Shop: Unneeded blanks fill a rack.
    Daily life: Buying food that expires before use.

    Motion: unnecessary movement by people

    Shop: An operator searches several drawers for a tool.
    Daily life: Searching for misplaced keys.

    Waiting: idle time before work can proceed

    Shop: A prepared job waits for missing information.
    Daily life: A completed form sits awaiting approval.

    Overproduction: too much or too early

    Shop: Extra parts are made without demand.
    Daily life: Printing copies nobody requested.

    Over-processing: work beyond requirements

    Shop: A hidden face receives an unnecessary cosmetic finish.
    Daily life: Entering the same information into duplicate lists.

    Defects: work that fails requirements

    Shop: An incorrect hole pattern requires a replacement part.
    Daily life: Retyping a form because of incorrect entries.

    Skills: unused talent

    Shop: An experienced operator's improvement idea is never considered.
    Daily life: Ignoring a team member's relevant skill when dividing work.

    Distinguish similar wastes before proposing a change; Practice

    Distinguish similar wastes before proposing a change

    Transportation follows material; motion follows people. Overproduction creates unwanted output; inventory is the resulting excess stock. Several wastes can occur together.

    Inspection is not automatically a defect, and every machine cycle is not automatically wasted time. Check Lean Value and Flow. Buffers may be needed for supply variation; removing them without understanding demand and reliability can interrupt delivery.

    Use 5S Workplace Organization to address searching and Kaizen and Standard Work to test a change. Improve the system rather than blaming the person caught in it.

    Practice waste classification

    Lean and Quality/Continuous Improvement

    Value Stream Mapping

    Show material and information flow, then distinguish process time from elapsed lead time.

    Map one product family from request to delivery

    Map one product family from request to delivery

    A value stream map (VSM) shows the steps and information that move a product or service toward the customer. Define the boundary and select work following a similar route. Walk the current process and record what happens, including queues and handoffs.

    Show who requests work, how instructions reach production, where material moves and where it waits. An operations-only map misses the information controlling those operations.

    Read process boxes, inventory triangles and flow arrows

    Read process boxes, inventory triangles and flow arrows

    This original sketch uses common conventions: a rectangle for a process, a triangle marked I for inventory, attached data boxes for measurements and arrows for flow. The legend distinguishes material movement from information. This is a teaching sketch, not a complete symbol standard.

    Measure elapsed lead time separately from process time; Interactive; Practice

    Measure elapsed lead time separately from process time

    Lead time is elapsed time through the stated boundary, including waits. Process time is time actively spent doing the work within that boundary. Not all processing adds customer value.

    Transfer size changes when jobs finish

    10 jobs; A = 4 min/job, B = 6 min/job. Compare transfer-all with transfer-one.

    Transfer all 10 jobs

    First item 46 minFull order 100 minProcessing / job 10 min

    Transfer 1 at a time

    First item 10 minFull order 64 minProcessing / job 10 min

    A is upper blue, B lower gold; bars are jobs, dashed lines completed-batch transfers. Minutes from order release 0; both plots share a scale.

    Job 10 with transfer-one: 36 min waiting before A + 0 held for batch + 18 waiting at B = 54 min waiting. Add 10 min processing: 64 min elapsed from order release 0.

    Ideal schedule: all equal jobs arrive at 0; serial single-job A then B, first come first served. A never blocks; waiting space is unlimited. Completed batches transfer immediately; the last may be smaller. Constant times; no setup, transport, failure, rework or variation. Finite-order illustration, not a factory forecast or a universal best batch.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 103 — Default 10-job example: exact transfer-one schedule.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 104 — Bounded model reference: scheduling equations and limits.

    The transfer-batch experiment above schedules a whole order. The earlier map sketch uses a fixed queue for one item:

    For one item in this simplified sequential example: cutting = 4 min, queue = 120 min, assembly = 6 min. Process time is 10 min; lead time is 130 min. No other delays or overlapping steps are included. Removing half the queue saves more elapsed time here than cutting one minute of processing.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 105 — A queue suggests a question, not a proven cause.

    Practice lead time

    Practice transfer batches

    Draw a future state and test a specific change

    Draw a future state and test a specific change

    A future-state map describes an improved flow to work toward. Choose a measurable change, assign responsibility and check the effect using Kaizen and Standard Work. Compare delivery, quality and workload across the whole stream.

    Lean and Quality/Continuous Improvement

    Kaizen and Standard Work

    Use small measured experiments to improve work and preserve what the team learns.

    Improve a specific problem with the people doing the work

    Improve a specific problem with the people doing the work

    Kaizen means continuous improvement. Start with an observed problem and a small change whose effect can be checked. Invite the people performing the task to explain what makes it difficult.

    For example, repeated searching for a shared measuring tool may suggest a labeled location. Measure search time and check whether the location also works for the next user. This is an illustrative experiment, not a promised productivity gain.

    Use Plan–Do–Check–Act to learn from a change

    Use Plan–Do–Check–Act to learn from a change

    1. Plan: define the problem, measure the starting condition and predict the effect of a proposed change.
    2. Do: try an authorized change on a manageable scale and record what happens.
    3. Check: compare results with the prediction, including quality and unintended effects.
    4. Act: adopt and document an improvement, revise an uncertain idea or undo an unsuccessful change; begin the next cycle.

    A useful result may be that the idea did not help. Keep that evidence rather than declaring success because something changed.

    Use standard work as a baseline that can improve; Checklist

    Use standard work as a baseline that can improve

    Standard work records the current agreed method so people can repeat it and recognize departures. State the sequence, relevant timing, checks and materials needed. In repetitive production, standardized work also relates the sequence and required in-process stock to the pace of customer demand.

    When an improvement is demonstrated, update the method and help everyone learn it. Do not bypass safety requirements or change controlled specifications as an informal experiment.

    • Record the problem and starting measure.
    • Describe one change and the expected result.
    • Test within applicable authorization and safety requirements.
    • Compare results and effects on other people or steps.
    • Update the agreed method if the evidence supports the change.

    Use 5S Workplace Organization for workplace organization and Eight Wastes: TIMWOODS to name problems.

    Supporting detail

    Addendum

    Additional evidence, standards context, and background referenced from the main text.

    1. Safety/Universal Rules/Electrical Safety

      Addendum 1. “It’s not the voltage that gets you, it’s the current”

      The saying is true. What usually gets taken from it — that the voltage does not matter — is not. Current is electricity actually moving through you, and it takes very little of it to do real harm. Volts sitting on a wire nobody is touching do nothing at all.

      Two things together decide how much current you get: how hard the electricity is being pushed, which is what voltage measures, and how hard your body holds it back, which is called resistance. Harder push, more current. More resistance, less.

      Your resistance is not a fixed number — wet skin holds current back far less than dry skin does, so the same push moves much more current through you. That half of it cannot be relied on, which is why the line is drawn on the half that can be: the push.

      Back to reference 1

    2. Safety/Universal Rules/Electrical Safety

      Addendum 2. The international standards are not one number

      On datasheets you will meet a different set of figures, and there the AC and DC limits are not the same:

      50 V AC / 120 V DC
      Extra-Low Voltage under IEC 61140 and IEC 60364-4-41 — 50 V AC rms, or 120 V ripple-free DC. “Ripple-free” is a real condition, not a figure of speech: past roughly 10 % rms ripple the supply is treated as AC and the lower number applies.
      30 V AC / 60 V DC
      Class ES1 in IEC 62368-1, the standard behind most benchtop and consumer equipment. ES1 is the class that needs no safeguard at all; ES2 runs up to 50 V AC / 120 V DC and requires one.

      Back to reference 2

    3. Safety/Universal Rules/Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets

      Addendum 3. All sixteen sections, and the four OSHA does not enforce

      This is OSHA's own list, from Appendix D to 29 CFR 1910.1200. The numbers and headings are fixed; a manufacturer cannot renumber them or reorder them.

      Section 1
      Identification — product identifier, recommended use and restrictions on use, who made it, emergency phone number.
      Section 2
      Hazard(s) identification — classification, signal word, hazard statement(s), symbol(s) and precautionary statement(s).
      Section 3
      Composition / information on ingredients — chemical name, CAS number, and for a mixture, the ingredients classified as health hazards and how much of each.
      Section 4
      First-aid measures — by route of exposure, plus the symptoms that matter and when to get medical attention.
      Section 5
      Fire-fighting measures — suitable and unsuitable extinguishing media, and what the chemical gives off when it burns.
      Section 6
      Accidental release measures — the spill response.
      Section 7
      Handling and storage — "conditions for safe storage, including any incompatibilities".
      Section 8
      Exposure controls / personal protection — the OSHA permissible exposure limit, the ACGIH threshold limit value, engineering controls, PPE.
      Section 9
      Physical and chemical properties — physical state, odor, flash point, auto-ignition temperature, density, pH and the rest.
      Section 10
      Stability and reactivity — reactivity, conditions to avoid, "incompatible materials", hazardous decomposition products.
      Section 11
      Toxicological information — the health effects and the data behind them, including any carcinogen listings.
      Section 12
      Ecological information
      Section 13
      Disposal considerations
      Section 14
      Transport information
      Section 15
      Regulatory information
      Section 16
      Other information — "the date of preparation of the SDS or the last change to it".

      Twelve through fifteen are the odd ones out. The headings have to be there: a note to the standard says an SDS "must also include the headings" for those four, "in order", to stay consistent with the international system the format comes from. What goes under them is a different question. Appendix D says "Sections 12-15 may be included in the SDS, but are not mandatory", and a second note to the same paragraph says "OSHA will not be enforcing information requirements in sections 12 through 15, as these areas are not under its jurisdiction."

      Those four cover the environment, waste, shipping and other agencies' regulations — EPA and DOT ground, not OSHA's. So Section 13 tells you what the manufacturer suggests doing with the leftovers. It does not tell you what happens to them here. Ask.

      Two more things about the shape of the document. The section order is fixed but the order within a section is not — preparers "are not required to present the information in any particular order within each section", so two sheets can look different inside the same numbered box. And a heading with nothing under it is not an oversight: where there is no relevant information, "the SDS shall clearly indicate that no applicable information is available." Read that as nobody has the data — not as nothing to worry about.

      Back to reference 3

    4. Safety/Universal Rules/Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets

      Addendum 4. Signal words, pictograms and H-numbers — how Section 2 is written

      There are exactly two signal words, and OSHA defines them in 1910.1200(c): a signal word indicates "the relative level of severity of hazard", and "'Danger' is used for the more severe hazards, while 'warning' is used for the less severe."

      Severity is relative to the same kind of hazard, and that is the part that catches people. Flammable liquids in OSHA's Appendix C are the clean example — all three categories carry the same Flame pictogram, and the signal word is the only thing separating them:

      Category 1
      Danger — "Extremely flammable liquid and vapor"
      Category 2
      Danger — "Highly flammable liquid and vapor"
      Category 3
      Warning — "Flammable liquid and vapor"

      So “warning” does not mean mild. A Category 3 flammable liquid still catches fire. The signal word ranks a hazard against others of its own kind; it is not a statement that the chemical is safe.

      The pictograms are a fixed set of eight — a black symbol in a red-bordered diamond standing on a point. OSHA names them: Flame, Flame Over Circle, Exclamation Mark, Exploding Bomb, Corrosion, Gas Cylinder, Health Hazard, and Skull and Crossbones.

      The H-numbers are an index, not the warning. Real sheets often print a code such as H225 beside a hazard statement. Those codes come from the international GHS scheme this format is built on, which treats them as reference labels rather than as a substitute for the statement itself. OSHA's Appendix C does not use them at all — it specifies the sentence. Read the sentence.

      Back to reference 4

    5. Safety/Universal Rules/Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets

      Addendum 5. Telling a current sheet from an old one

      Section 16 carries "the date of preparation of the SDS or the last change to it." That is the only date on the document, and it is how you tell a live sheet from one that has sat in a binder for a decade.

      Keeping it current is the manufacturer's job, not yours. Under 1910.1200(g)(5), when a manufacturer or importer "becomes newly aware of any significant information regarding the hazards of a chemical, or ways to protect against the hazards, this new information shall be added to the safety data sheet within three months."

      Back to reference 5

    6. Safety/Universal Rules/Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets

      Addendum 6. What makes a flammables cabinet “approved”, and how to spot one

      OSHA calls it a storage cabinet and defines it by a fire test rather than by how solid it looks. 29 CFR 1910.106(d)(3) requires cabinets to "limit the internal temperature to not more than 325 °F. when subjected to a 10-minute fire test", with all joints and seams staying tight and the door staying closed throughout.

      The same paragraph requires the marking, which is the fastest way to recognise one: "Cabinets shall be labeled in conspicuous lettering, 'Flammable - Keep Fire Away.'"

      Back to reference 6

    7. Safety/Universal Rules/Machine Hazards and Housekeeping

      Addendum 7. The word for this, and where it comes from

      “Nip point” is not shop slang. It is the term the machine-guarding standard uses. 29 CFR 1910.212(a)(1) requires guarding against “hazards such as those created by point of operation, ingoing nip points, rotating parts, flying chips and sparks.”

      OSHA’s Machine Guarding eTool puts it plainly: “In-running nip point hazards are caused by the rotating parts on machinery.” Its longer treatment, Concepts and Techniques of Machine Safeguarding (OSHA 3067), gives three kinds:

      • “Parts can rotate in opposite directions while their axes are parallel to each other. These parts may be in contact (producing a nip point) or in close proximity.” — meshing gears.
      • “Nip points are also created between rotating and tangentially moving parts. Some examples would be: the point of contact between a power transmission belt and its pulley, a chain and a sprocket, and a rack and pinion.”
      • “Nip points can occur between rotating and fixed parts which create a shearing, crushing, or abrading action.”

      So belts, chains, sprockets and gears are rotating hazards by name. What makes them dangerous is that they draw material in — not that two parts close on each other.

      OSHA is just as direct about the plain shaft: “Rotating motion can be dangerous; even smooth, slowly rotating shafts can grip hair and clothing, and through minor contact force the hand and arm into a dangerous position.”

      These parts are meant to be behind covers, and the standard is specific about it — 29 CFR 1910.219(f)(3): “All sprocket wheels and chains shall be enclosed unless they are more than seven (7) feet above the floor or platform.”

      Back to reference 7

    8. Safety/Universal Rules/Machine Hazards and Housekeeping

      Addendum 8. What the investigations actually describe

      Oregon’s state fatality-investigation program, summarizing the record for this class of machine: “The most common causes of death and injury from metal lathes include entanglement of clothing in moving parts, being hit by loose objects on the lathe (e.g., chuck keys, tools, metal shavings) and being struck by a part that has not been adequately secured.” (OR-FACE 2012-18-1, Experienced Journeyman Machinist Killed While Operating an Engine Lathe, 2014.)

      Four investigated deaths, all the same event — something attached to a person touched something turning, and the machine did the rest:

      • Smoothing a part while it turned. A 69-year-old machinist with over 30 years’ experience “reached over the work piece to smooth out a radiused transition with emery cloth and a file in hand” and “his loose clothing (left arm sleeve) became entangled around the rotating work piece”. A co-worker 30 feet away heard “a strange ‘winding-up’ sound”. Of that same part, the shop foreman had said that “the rough surface could grab clothing or gloves”. (OR-FACE 2012-18-1.)
      • Stock sticking out the back of the spindle. A 52-year-old machinist was set up on a 103-inch steel bar: “Due to the length of the material, 24 inches were sticking out the back of the lathe, unguarded, and held in place with a clamping device that rotates as the lathe rotates.” He reached across the running machine and “the sleeve of his shirt became entangled”. (Kentucky FACE 21KY002, 2021.)
      • A burr on the end of the bar. A lathe operator in his twenties had a 1 7/8-inch stub of 1-inch bar standing past the tailstock. “The right pocket of his shirt was caught by the rotating tailstock burr. His shirt wrapped around the stock and tightened at the decedent’s neck and chest.” The listed contributing factor is “walking to and/or reaching over unguarded rotating bar stock”. OSHA makes the same point in general: the danger “increases when projections such as set screws, bolts, nicks, abrasions, and projecting keys… are exposed on rotating parts.” (Michigan FACE 14MI034, 2014; OSHA Machine Guarding eTool.)
      • A drill press. “As Employee #1 reached into the unguarded point of operation, his shirt sleeve or gloves became entangled in the drill bit. Employee #1 was pulled toward the machine, entangling Employee #1’s long hair. The drill press continued to spin, completely pulling Employee #1 into the operating area.” She died of her injuries. The same report records that the spindle “had speeds that ranged from 45 to 1115 rotations per minute”. (OSHA accident 114097.015, 20 February 2019.)

      Why abrasive cloth keeps appearing. The UK Health and Safety Executive publishes a sheet on this one task: “Every year there are serious accidents involving the use of emery cloth on metalworking lathes. These accidents result in serious injuries such as broken bones, dislocations, lacerations, amputations and occasionally death.” The mechanism it names is the one above: “Accidents occur when hand-held emery cloth is entangled in the rotating parts of the machine or where the emery cloth is snagged on the rotating component dragging the operator into the danger zone.” Its own rules are that emery cloth “should NEVER be applied directly by hand on manual metalworking lathes”, and that gloves “increase the risk of entanglement and” are “never acceptable near rotating parts of machinery”. (HSE Engineering Information Sheet No 2, rev 1, 2015 — that is HSE’s guidance; ask what the procedure is in the shop you are standing in.)

      And the drill press is not the exception it looks like. OSHA’s own drill-press training script lists, among the ways accidents happen, “getting dangling jewelry, loose clothing, or hair caught in the drill chuck (rotational hazard)”, and states: “The primary hazards of drill presses are contact at the point of operation and rotational hazards. An operator can risk serious hand injury when working too close to the drilling area, wearing gloves, loose clothing, loose hair, or jewelry.”

      Back to reference 8

    9. Safety/Universal Rules/Machine Hazards and Housekeeping

      Addendum 9. Why belts and chains count as rotating, not pinching

      OSHA sorts machine hazards by the motion that causes them, and “pinch point” is the vocabulary it attaches to parts that travel, not to parts that turn. From Concepts and Techniques of Machine Safeguarding (OSHA 3067):

      • Reciprocating motion — “Reciprocating motions may be hazardous because, during the back-and-forth or up-and-down motion, a worker may be struck by or caught between a moving and a stationary part.”
      • Transverse motion, which means movement in a straight continuous line — “Transverse motion (movement in a straight, continuous line) creates a hazard because a worker may be struck or caught in a pinch or shear point by the moving part.”

      A belt on a pulley is a rotating hazard that draws material in; a table running up against a column is a moving hazard that closes on it. Both can take a hand, and the vocabulary is worth keeping straight because the two do not have the same tell. You avoid the first by giving it nothing to grip. You avoid the second by knowing where the gap is going.

      Back to reference 9

    10. Safety/Universal Rules/Machine Hazards and Housekeeping

      Addendum 10. Why the rule has no exceptions in it

      Guarding is not a local preference. 29 CFR 1910.212(a)(1) — quoted already in Rotating machinery above for its definition of a nip point — is a guarding requirement first: one or more methods of machine guarding shall be provided to protect the operator and other employees from hazards including those created by point of operation, ingoing nip points, rotating parts, flying chips and sparks.

      The reason a rule like this is written without exceptions is that the exceptions are exactly where people get hurt. A guard comes off for a legitimate setup, the setup takes longer than expected, somebody else walks up to a machine that looks normal and is not. The standard's own answer to “but this task genuinely needs the guard off” is not a more careful operator — it is Lockout/Tagout, the next card on this page, which is a procedure rather than a permission.

      Back to reference 10

    11. Safety/Universal Rules/Machine Hazards and Housekeeping

      Addendum 11. What the standard actually covers

      29 CFR 1910.147(a)(1)(i): “This standard covers the servicing and maintenance of machines and equipment in which the unexpected energization or start up of the machines or equipment, or release of stored energy could cause injury to employees.”

      Two things are worth reading twice. Unexpected is the whole point — the hazard is not that the machine runs, it is that it runs while someone has a hand inside it. And stored energy is named alongside energization, because a machine that has been switched off and unplugged can still contain everything it needs to move once.

      “Servicing and maintenance” is much broader than it sounds. The standard defines it as “constructing, installing, setting up, adjusting, inspecting, modifying, and maintaining and/or servicing machines or equipment”, and adds: “These activities include lubrication, cleaning or unjamming of machines or equipment and making adjustments or tool changes, where the employee may be exposed to the unexpected energization or startup of the equipment or release of hazardous energy.” Setting up, clearing a jam and changing a tool are all on that list.

      Stored energy gets its own requirement — 1910.147(d)(5)(i): “Following the application of lockout or tagout devices to energy isolating devices, all potentially hazardous stored or residual energy shall be relieved, disconnected, restrained, and otherwise rendered safe.” The lock comes first, and then the energy already in the machine is dealt with. Both, in that order.

      Back to reference 11

    12. Safety/Universal Rules/Machine Hazards and Housekeeping

      Addendum 12. Why the chuck key rule is worded as a grip and not as a reminder

      A key left in a chuck is launched the instant the machine starts. Written as “remember to remove the key” the rule depends on you remembering at the one moment you are busy with something else; written as the key never leaves your hand there is nothing to remember, because a key that is still in the chuck is still in your hand and you cannot start the machine.

      Do not let a spring be the thing that saves you. Some chuck keys are spring-loaded and eject themselves when you let go — ours are, on the lathe. Not all keys are, and our Jacobs chuck keys are not. So the habit has to be the same on every machine, or it is a habit that works until you walk up to a different chuck.

      A drill-press chuck key is lighter than a lathe chuck key and carries far less energy. It is still dangerous: it is in the list of things that become projectiles in Rotating machinery above, and “less mass” is not the same as “will not hurt you” when it leaves a spinning chuck at the distance you are standing.

      Back to reference 12

    13. Safety/Universal Rules/Fire Safety

      Addendum 13. Why dry sand is on the list, and why it is probably not on yours

      Sand does work. The Aluminum Association’s Guidelines for Handling Aluminum Fines (F-1) lists fine dry sand, “preferably finer than 20 mesh,” next to approved dry powders as effective for isolating an aluminum fines fire. It also says what has to be true first.

      • Dry. F-1 says dry sand. Damp sand is water, and water “will react with the aluminum fines to form flammable hydrogen gas.”
      • Already in the room. “A plentiful supply should be easily available in the operating area and stored in covered bins or drums.” Sand fetched after the fire starts is not that.
      • With the right tool waiting beside it. “Long handled shovels should be available at each bin or drum, and should be constructed of non-sparking metal.”
      • Laid, not thrown. The shovels “lay the sand or powder around the edge or perimeter of the fire.” You are walling it in. Anything thrown at the pile raises the dust cloud that is the actual explosion.
      • Decided before it started, by someone senior. “Qualified supervisory personnel should decide in advance whether it is better to attempt to fight the fire or to withdraw to a safe location and allow it to burn itself out.”

      Those are preconditions, not tips. If you cannot point at the covered sand bin and the non-sparking shovel beside it right now, you do not have this option — and the call to fight it was never yours to make on the spot. Alarm, evacuate, report.

      Back to reference 13

    14. Safety/Equipment/Table Saw

      Addendum 14. Why one feed rate does not fit every cut

      Thickness, wood, blade and available power change how readily material cuts. Pushing harder does not fix binding or a poorly chosen setup; it can make control worse.

      Back to reference 14

    15. Safety/Equipment/Band Saw

      Addendum 15. Why thickness matters as well as material

      A thin section needs enough teeth engaged to avoid snagging; a thick section also needs room between teeth to carry chips away. Select the blade for both conditions rather than assuming all metal needs the same high TPI.

      Back to reference 15

    16. Safety/Equipment/Drill Press

      Addendum 16. Why larger drills usually need fewer revolutions per minute

      At the same spindle speed, a larger bit's outer edge travels faster. Diameter, work material and bit material all affect the speed choice. “Larger or harder means slower” is a starting trend, not a speed setting.

      Back to reference 16

    17. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/What Is Manufacturing?

      Addendum 17. Why the boundary needs context

      Different industries draw the primary/secondary boundary differently. Here, use the raw-resource-to-stock and stock-to-part distinction. Extraction supplies the raw resource; mining alone does not turn ore into an ingot. A supplier's finished product can also be the next manufacturer's starting material.

      Back to reference 17

    18. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Manufacturing Process Categories

      Addendum 18. A laser cut does not have to vaporize all the removed material

      Material may melt and be expelled from the cut; vaporization can also contribute. The classification depends on removal, not on which thermal mechanism dominates. TWI explains melt removal in laser cutting.

      Back to reference 18

    19. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Material Families

      Addendum 19. Why another book may show a different family list

      Other books may give composites a separate family, split glass from ceramics, or organize materials by bonding and structure. This collection keeps the instructor's four-family model. Engineered composites belong within Wood & Composites, including composites with no wood in them.

      Some materials fit more than one description. In the course's examples, plain concrete sits with Ceramics & Glass; steel-reinforced concrete illustrates Wood & Composites when the combined material system is the subject. Concrete itself also has a composite structure. State what is being classified rather than treating these labels as mutually exclusive scientific definitions.

      Back to reference 19

    20. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Material Families

      Addendum 20. A supplier value that checks the floating claim

      Plaskolite's OPTIX acrylic data lists a relative density of 1.19, with water as the comparison. This supports the conclusion that a solid piece is denser than water. Family descriptions are screening guides; use the actual grade's data for a design.

      Back to reference 20

    21. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Material Families

      Addendum 21. Hard to machine does not mean impossible to machine

      Corning's MACOR glass-ceramic is specifically designed for machining with conventional metalworking tools. That is a useful counterexample to a blanket claim that ceramics cannot be worked after forming.

      Back to reference 21

    22. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Material Properties

      Addendum 22. Stress, strain and modulus give the comparison units

      For a simple axial test, engineering stress is force divided by original cross-sectional area. Engineering strain is change in length divided by original length. Stress has units such as MPa; strain is a ratio with no unit.

      In a linear elastic region, the slope of stress against strain is Young's modulus, a measure of material stiffness. Yield strength concerns permanent deformation; ultimate tensile strength is the highest engineering tensile stress reached in the test. A nonlinear curve does not, by itself, prove that a material has no yield behavior.

      See Measurement Language for writing quantities and units consistently.

      Back to reference 22

    23. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Material Properties

      Addendum 23. Why a single “toughness number” needs its test method

      The area under a tensile stress–strain curve through fracture measures energy absorbed per original volume in that test. Impact tests and fracture-toughness tests describe related but different behavior. Temperature, loading rate and flaws can change the result, so compare like tests.

      Back to reference 23

    24. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Material Properties

      Addendum 24. Not every material has one useful melting-point number

      Pure crystalline substances can have a sharp melting point; many alloys melt over a range. Glass and amorphous thermoplastics soften over a range rather than showing a sharp crystalline melting transition. Thermosets and wood decompose rather than melting into a reusable processing liquid. Use material-specific processing and service data.

      Back to reference 24

    25. Materials and Manufacturing Processes/Foundations/Additive Manufacturing Process Families

      Addendum 25. Vocabulary, brand attribution and source scope

      ISO/ASTM 52900:2021 is the current fundamentals-and-vocabulary standard and describes additive shaping as successive addition of material. Its public abstract does not reproduce the full family list. The family structure and readable mechanisms here are checked against the NIST AM technology overview and the seven-family discussion in ORNL's Additive Manufacturing Design Guidelines. Stratasys's legal terms identify FDM as a registered trademark and PolyJet as a trademark; its PolyJet technology page documents the bounded photopolymer-droplet, UV-cure and support example used here. This page paraphrases sources and uses original graphics rather than copied standard or vendor art.

      Back to reference 25
